meta.blurb: Go and watch an ant, says one old saying, and learn how to work. The Book of Proverbs holds ancient Israel's short, sharp advice on money, friends, words and temper, and a wisdom that calls out loudly in the market square.
meta.bible: Proverbs: a book of the Hebrew Bible, also part of the Christian Old Testament, made of short sayings and longer poems about wisdom. Solomon: the king of ancient Israel, famous for his wisdom, to whom tradition credits many of the sayings. Israel: the ancient kingdom and people where the book began. Wisdom: pictured in the book as a woman who calls out to everyone. Folly: Wisdom's opposite, also pictured as a woman. The Lord: the name the book uses for God. Hezekiah: a king of Judah whose men, the book says, copied out more of Solomon's proverbs. Agur: the writer of the thirtieth chapter. Bible. Hebrew. Judah. Chapters one to nine: a father speaking to his son. Chapters ten to twenty-two: short two-line sayings. The Sayings of the Wise: a section that begins in chapter twenty-two. Chapter thirty-one: the poem of the capable woman. Voice and tone: calm, warm, practical and respectful. Every saying is attributed to the book. The words are the book's own ideas retold, never long quotations. Where a saying can be understood in more than one way, say so. Never preach or compare faiths. Lemuel: a king whose mother's advice fills the first part of chapter thirty-one; nothing else is known of him. Jakeh: the father of Agur. Agur's chapter: sayings and riddles built on numbers, such as three things and four. Instruction of Amenemope: an Egyptian teaching that scholars compare with part of the Sayings of the Wise. Job and Ecclesiastes: other books of the Hebrew Bible that ask harder questions about wisdom. Egypt. Chapters ten to twenty-two and twenty-five to twenty-nine: sayings that are often set in pairs or opposites. Chapter thirty-one, verses ten to thirty-one: an alphabet poem in which each line begins with the next Hebrew letter. Pages never copy long lines from the book; they retell its ideas in new words.

beats.scene: A scribe writes short sayings on a scroll by lamplight
beats.summary: The Book of Proverbs is introduced as a collection of short sayings, each holding a lesson.

beats.scene: King Solomon sits among scrolls while scribes copy his words
beats.summary: Tradition links the book with Solomon, though other writers and later copyists appear in it.

beats.scene: A teacher speaks to a mixed group of young and old listeners
beats.summary: The opening lines say why the book was written and who it is for.

beats.scene: A young woman stands on a quiet hill as the dawn rises
beats.summary: Respect for the Lord is called the beginning of knowledge, and fools despise wisdom.

beats.scene: A boy listens as his mother and father speak at a table
beats.summary: A father begins his long talk by asking his son to heed both parents.

beats.scene: A young man stops on a dark path while a group beckons
beats.summary: A gang invites the son to join them and share the stolen goods.

beats.scene: A bird flies away from a net spread openly on the ground
beats.summary: The father warns that the schemers are really trapping themselves.

beats.scene: A woman stands in a busy market square and calls to the crowd
beats.summary: Wisdom is pictured as a woman who calls out in the streets to everyone.

beats.scene: A closed door stands in the street as a storm gathers
beats.summary: Wisdom warns that people who ignore her will find no help when trouble comes.

beats.scene: A family sleeps peacefully in a quiet house under the stars
beats.summary: Whoever listens to Wisdom will live in safety and be at ease.

beats.scene: A miner digs in rocky ground with a small lamp beside him
beats.summary: The father says wisdom must be sought like hidden silver.

beats.scene: A guard stands at a narrow gate holding a shield at night
beats.summary: The Lord is the source of wisdom and shields the honest.

beats.scene: A young man walks along a clear path carrying a lamp
beats.summary: Wisdom brings an understanding of what is right, just and fair.

beats.scene: A bright straight road runs beside a dark and twisting one
beats.summary: Wisdom saves the young man from people who speak twisted words and love the dark.

beats.scene: A young man hesitates in a doorway while a lantern flickers
beats.summary: Wisdom warns him against flattery that tempts a person to break the promise of marriage.

beats.scene: A farmer stands in a green valley beside his small house
beats.summary: Honest people will live safely in the land, but the wicked will lose it.

beats.scene: A young man writes on a small tablet beside his front door
beats.summary: The son is told to keep his father's teaching, love and faithfulness close.

beats.scene: A traveller walks a winding path between two green hills
beats.summary: Trust the Lord with all your heart, and he will make your paths straight.

beats.scene: A farmer carries a basket of grain past a full barn
beats.summary: Honour the Lord with wealth and the first of the harvest.

beats.scene: A father rests a hand on his son's shoulder beside a fire
beats.summary: The Lord's correction is compared to a father's care for the son he loves.

beats.scene: Jewels and silver coins lie beside a glowing lamp on a table
beats.summary: Whoever finds wisdom is happy, for she is worth more than silver, gold or rubies.

beats.scene: A tree heavy with fruit stands in a sunlit garden
beats.summary: Wisdom holds long life, riches and honour, and is a tree of life to those who hold her.

beats.scene: Dawn light spreads over hills, a wide sea and drifting clouds
beats.summary: The Lord is said to have made the earth and the heavens by wisdom.

beats.scene: A man sleeps peacefully in a plain bed as moonlight enters the window
beats.summary: Those who keep good judgment walk safely and sleep without fear.

beats.scene: A man at his gate hands a sack of grain to a neighbour
beats.summary: Do not hold back help from a neighbour, plot against him or envy the violent.

beats.scene: A small house glows with warm light while a grand house stands dark
beats.summary: The Lord blesses the homes of the righteous, and he favours the humble.

beats.scene: An old man talks to his grown son beside a fire
beats.summary: The father tells how his own father once taught him to hold on to wisdom.

beats.scene: A young man bows his head as a woman places a crown on it
beats.summary: Get wisdom and understanding, whatever the cost, and she will honour you.

beats.scene: A bright path of dawn light runs beside a dark road
beats.summary: The path of the righteous is like dawn, but the way of the wicked is deep darkness.

beats.scene: A spring of clear water flows from a rock beside a straight road
beats.summary: Guard your heart, keep your speech honest and look straight ahead.

beats.scene: A honeycomb drips on a table beside a bitter green plant
beats.summary: The flatterer's words are sweet as honey but end as bitter as poison.

beats.scene: An old man sits alone at a bare table, head in hands
beats.summary: The father warns that unfaithfulness costs a person strength, years and wealth.

beats.scene: A husband and wife draw water from a well in a garden
beats.summary: Faithfulness in marriage is pictured as drinking from your own well.

beats.scene: An old couple sit hand in hand as the sun sets over their garden
beats.summary: The father tells his son to be happy with his wife, for the Lord sees every path.

beats.scene: A worried man looks at a signed paper while a neighbour waits
beats.summary: Anyone who has promised to pay a neighbour's debt is told to get free quickly.

beats.scene: A single ant carries a seed along a sandy path
beats.summary: The lazy person is told to learn from the hard-working ant.

beats.scene: A man sleeps in a chair while weeds creep over his field
beats.summary: Too much sleep lets poverty arrive like a robber.

beats.scene: A man winks and taps his foot while onlookers watch him coldly
beats.summary: A troublemaker plans evil and stirs up quarrels, and disaster will fall on him.

beats.scene: A teacher counts on his fingers while his students watch
beats.summary: The book lists the first three of seven things that the Lord hates.

beats.scene: A teacher raises four fingers while students count along
beats.summary: The list ends with wicked plans, feet that hurry to harm, false witnesses and people who stir up quarrels.

beats.scene: A lamp glows on a table beside a folded scroll at night
beats.summary: The commands of a father and the teaching of a mother are called a lamp for the way.

beats.scene: A man draws his hand back from a bed of glowing coals
beats.summary: The father warns that playing with temptation is like carrying fire in your lap.

beats.scene: A thief is caught taking bread at a market stall
beats.summary: A hungry thief can repay what he took, but harm to a marriage cannot be repaid.

beats.scene: A young man ties a cord around his finger as a reminder
beats.summary: The son is told to guard the teaching as the apple of his eye.

beats.scene: A man looks through a lattice window at a young man walking at dusk
beats.summary: The writer tells what he saw from his window: a young man without sense walking toward danger.

beats.scene: A woman in fine clothes meets a young man at a dim street corner
beats.summary: A woman who lingers at every corner meets him with flattering words.

beats.scene: A woman beckons toward a door with fine linen at the window
beats.summary: She says that her husband is away and invites him to come in.

beats.scene: A bird flutters toward a hidden snare at the edge of a road
beats.summary: He follows her without seeing the danger, like an ox, a deer or a bird.

beats.scene: A road runs downhill toward a dark doorway at dusk
beats.summary: The father begs his sons not to stray onto her road, which leads to the grave.

beats.scene: Two women stand at opposite ends of one street calling to passers-by
beats.summary: Wisdom and the flatterer both call from the street, but their roads lead to different places.

beats.scene: A woman stands on a hill beside the city gate calling to the crowd
beats.summary: In the eighth chapter Wisdom calls from the heights and the gates to all who will listen.

beats.scene: A silver coin and a ruby rest on a table beside an open scroll
beats.summary: Wisdom says that her words are true and that she is worth more than silver or rubies.

beats.scene: A king and his advisers sit at a table listening to a calm voice
beats.summary: Wisdom says that kings and rulers govern well by her help.

beats.scene: An old man and a girl find a small gate in a garden wall
beats.summary: Wisdom loves those who love her, and those who look for her find her.

beats.scene: A sunrise spreads over a calm empty sea with mountains in the mist
beats.summary: Wisdom says that the Lord made her first, before the oceans and the mountains.

beats.scene: A young woman watches a builder draw a great circle over the sea
beats.summary: Wisdom is pictured beside the Lord as the world was made, full of delight.

beats.scene: A man waits patiently at a doorway in the early morning light
beats.summary: Those who listen to Wisdom and wait at her door find life.

beats.scene: A long table is set inside a house with seven stone pillars
beats.summary: Wisdom builds a house with seven pillars, sets a feast and invites the simple.

beats.scene: A wise man listens quietly while a mocker turns away in anger
beats.summary: A mocker hates correction, but the wise grow wiser from it.

beats.scene: A loud woman sits on her doorstep calling to people passing by
beats.summary: Folly calls from her doorway too, but her guests do not know where she leads.

beats.scene: A mother and father greet their son at the door of the house
beats.summary: The short sayings of Solomon begin, and the first speaks of a wise son and a foolish one.

beats.scene: A thief hides a bag of coins in rocky ground at night
beats.summary: Wealth gained by wrong does not last, and the Lord does not let the honest go hungry.

beats.scene: One son harvests a field while another sleeps under a tree
beats.summary: Hard work brings wealth, and the son who sleeps through the harvest brings shame.

beats.scene: Villagers gather quietly around the grave of a kind old man
beats.summary: The memory of a good person is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot.

beats.scene: One man walks a straight road while another stumbles on a crooked path
beats.summary: Honest people walk in safety, but those who take crooked ways are found out.

beats.scene: Two friends sit on a bench, one with an arm around the other
beats.summary: Hatred stirs up trouble, but love covers over every wrong.

beats.scene: A high stone wall surrounds a rich house while a poor man passes by
beats.summary: Wealth is a city wall to the rich, while poverty ruins the poor; listening to correction leads to life.

beats.scene: A man sits quietly at a table while others talk loudly
beats.summary: Many words lead to trouble, but the lips of the righteous feed many.

beats.scene: A storm passes over a village and one house remains standing on rock
beats.summary: After the storm the wicked are gone, but the righteous stand firm.

beats.scene: A tree with deep roots grows in a field at sunrise
beats.summary: Respect for the Lord brings years and joy, and the righteous will never be uprooted.

beats.scene: A merchant weighs grain on a fair set of brass scales
beats.summary: The Lord hates dishonest scales and is pleased by accurate weights.

beats.scene: A proud man in fine clothes walks past a quiet man
beats.summary: Pride is followed by shame, but wisdom is found with the humble.

beats.scene: A man with a heavy purse stops at a river while another crosses
beats.summary: Riches cannot rescue a person on the day of trouble, but doing right can.

beats.scene: A town square is full of banners, music and dancing
beats.summary: When the righteous do well the whole city rejoices.

beats.scene: Two neighbours whisper over a fence while a third walks quietly by
beats.summary: A gossip betrays secrets, but a trustworthy person keeps them.

beats.scene: A king listens to three advisers around a wooden table
beats.summary: A nation is safe when it has many good advisers.

beats.scene: A woman helps an old man carry water up a hill
beats.summary: A kind woman gains honour, and kind people do good to themselves.

beats.scene: A woman shares bread with neighbours who gather at her door
beats.summary: The generous grow richer, and whoever refreshes others will be refreshed.

beats.scene: One tree has green leaves while another in the same field is bare
beats.summary: Those who trust in riches fall, but the righteous grow like green leaves.

beats.scene: A pig wearing a gold ring stands in a muddy farmyard
beats.summary: Beauty without good sense is like a gold ring in a pig's nose.

beats.scene: A student nods as a teacher holding a scroll corrects his work
beats.summary: Whoever loves correction loves knowledge, and no one is made safe by wickedness.

beats.scene: A modest man eats bread while a boaster sits at an empty table
beats.summary: A good wife is her husband's crown, and it is better to live simply than to pretend to be great.

beats.scene: A farmer gives water to his ox in the early morning
beats.summary: The righteous care for their animals, and whoever works the land has plenty.

beats.scene: A man calmly ignores an insult shouted by a loud neighbour
beats.summary: A fool shows his anger at once, but a sensible person overlooks an insult.

beats.scene: A healer bandages a hand while a quarrel rages nearby
beats.summary: Reckless words cut like a sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.

beats.scene: A woman speaks softly to a worried friend beside a window
beats.summary: A kind word cheers a heart weighed down by worry.

beats.scene: A hunter prepares a meal while a lazy man sits by a cold fire
beats.summary: Diligent hands will rule, but the lazy will work for others.

beats.scene: A boy listens closely to his father at the door of the house
beats.summary: A wise child heeds his father's teaching, and whoever guards his lips guards his life.

beats.scene: A man drops one coin at a time into a clay jar
beats.summary: Quick wealth shrinks, but wealth gathered little by little grows.

beats.scene: Three travellers walk together along a country road at dusk
beats.summary: Hope put off makes the heart sick, and whoever walks with the wise grows wise.

beats.scene: A woman lays stones for a wall beside her house
beats.summary: A wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one tears it down.

beats.scene: An ox pulls a plough across a field behind an empty clean barn
beats.summary: A clean barn means no oxen, but an ox's strength brings a great harvest.

beats.scene: A man stands where a pleasant path and a rough path divide
beats.summary: There is a way that seems right, but it ends badly, and even laughter can hide an aching heart.

beats.scene: A man takes a deep breath and lowers his raised fist
beats.summary: The patient have great understanding, and a calm heart gives life to the body.

beats.scene: A well-dressed man gives bread to a poor child at the roadside
beats.summary: Whoever is kind to the needy honours their Maker.

beats.scene: A carpenter works busily at his bench while two men chat idly
beats.summary: All hard work brings a profit, but mere talk brings poverty.

beats.scene: A banner flies above the walls of a peaceful city at sunrise
beats.summary: Righteousness lifts up a nation, and a king is pleased with a wise servant.

beats.scene: A woman answers a shouting man calmly, and his face softens
beats.summary: A gentle answer turns away anger.

beats.scene: A family laughs over a simple bowl of vegetables at a small table
beats.summary: A little with love is better than a feast with hatred.

beats.scene: A young man and an old woman talk over a plan at a table
beats.summary: Plans succeed with many advisers, and humility comes before honour.

beats.scene: A man sketches a plan on a scroll, then looks up at the stars
beats.summary: People make plans in their hearts, but the Lord directs their steps.

beats.scene: A tall tower leans and cracks above a proud man
beats.summary: Pride goes before destruction, and a humble life is better than shared plunder.

beats.scene: A king sits on a simple throne as petitioners bring letters
beats.summary: A king delights in honest lips, and his favour is like a spring rain cloud.

beats.scene: A honeycomb sits on a plate beside a cup of water
beats.summary: Wisdom is better than gold, and pleasant words are sweet as honey.

beats.scene: A whispering man tugs a friend's sleeve toward a dark alley
beats.summary: A troublemaker plots evil, stirs up quarrels and leads his neighbour astray.

beats.scene: An old man with grey hair sits at the town gate, greeted warmly
beats.summary: Grey hair is a crown, and a patient person is better than a warrior.

beats.scene: A family eats dry bread together while a grandfather holds a baby
beats.summary: A dry crust with peace is better than a feast with strife.

beats.scene: A man opens a small gap in a dam and water pours out
beats.summary: Starting a quarrel is like breaking a dam, and forgiving keeps friends.

beats.scene: Two friends carry a heavy basket together along a hillside path
beats.summary: A friend loves at all times, and a cheerful heart is good medicine.

beats.scene: A man with a finger over his lips stands among a loud crowd
beats.summary: A person who holds back his words seems wise, even if he is a fool.

beats.scene: A man sits alone at a window while a crowd passes below
beats.summary: A person who stays apart seeks only his own wishes, and a fool loves only his own opinions.

beats.scene: A tall stone tower stands on a hill as people run toward it
beats.summary: The name of the Lord is a strong tower, while the rich trust in imagined walls.

beats.scene: A young man cuts off an older man's words while a woman frowns
beats.summary: Humility comes before honour, and answering before listening is foolish.

beats.scene: Two men argue before a judge at the city gate
beats.summary: A strong spirit carries a person through sickness, and the first to speak seems right until questioned.

beats.scene: Two brothers sit apart with their backs turned before a stone wall
beats.summary: A wronged brother is harder to win back than a fortified city.

beats.scene: A woman speaks kindly to a crying child while a man shouts nearby
beats.summary: The tongue has the power of life and death.

beats.scene: A poor man knocks at a rich man's door, a friend beside him
beats.summary: The poor plead for mercy, but a true friend sticks closer than a brother.

beats.scene: A poor man walks steadily while a rich man hurries and trips
beats.summary: It is better to be poor and honest than a crooked fool, and haste misses the way.

beats.scene: A rich man sits among many friends while a poor man stands alone
beats.summary: Wealth brings many friends, but the poor are often left alone.

beats.scene: A man offers his coat to a shivering traveller by the roadside
beats.summary: Overlooking an offence is glorious, and kindness to the poor is a loan to the Lord.

beats.scene: A man sleeps in the shade while his field stands bare
beats.summary: A lazy person will not lift food to his mouth, and strong drink leads the unwise astray.

beats.scene: A man lowers a bucket into a deep well
beats.summary: A person's purposes are deep water, and a person of insight draws them out.

beats.scene: A father walks with his small children along a hillside path
beats.summary: Many claim unfailing love, but a righteous person's children are blessed after him.

beats.scene: A buyer waves away fruit at a stall, then walks off smiling
beats.summary: A buyer runs down the goods, then boasts, and bread gained by cheating turns to gravel.

beats.scene: Gold and rubies lie on a table beside a wise old woman
beats.summary: Wise lips are a rarer jewel than gold, and the Lord will deal with wrongs.

beats.scene: A small lamp lights the inside of a dark room
beats.summary: The human spirit is the lamp of the Lord, and the old are honoured for their grey hair.

beats.scene: A farmer opens a small channel to guide a stream through his field
beats.summary: A king's heart is like a stream in the Lord's hand, and doing right is better than sacrifice.

beats.scene: A man covers his ears as a poor woman calls at his door
beats.summary: Whoever ignores the cry of the poor will not be heard in his own trouble.

beats.scene: A man eats bread alone on the corner of a flat roof
beats.summary: It is better to live on a roof corner than with quarrels, and victory belongs to the Lord.

beats.scene: A mother walks hand in hand with a small child along a path
beats.summary: A good name is worth more than riches, and a child should be taught the right way.

beats.scene: A scribe teaches a young student with a scroll in a sunny courtyard
beats.summary: A new section begins, the Sayings of the Wise, urging the reader to listen and trust the Lord.

beats.scene: A poor farmer stands before a judge while a hot-tempered man glares
beats.summary: Do not rob the poor or crush the needy, and do not befriend the quick-tempered.

beats.scene: A craftsman works skilfully at his bench while a king's servant watches
beats.summary: Do not make hasty pledges for debts, and skilful workers will serve before kings.

beats.scene: A young man sits politely at a rich banquet and eats little
beats.summary: At a ruler's table take care, and do not crave fine food.

beats.scene: A tired merchant counts coins at night beside a candle
beats.summary: Do not wear yourself out to get rich, for riches can vanish like a bird in flight.

beats.scene: A farmer looks at an ancient boundary stone marking his field
beats.summary: Do not move an ancient boundary stone or take the fields of orphans.

beats.scene: A father and mother watch their grown son return through the gate
beats.summary: A wise child gladdens his parents, and the truth is worth buying and never selling.

beats.scene: A man looks at a splendid house across the road, then walks on
beats.summary: Do not envy evildoers, for a house is built by wisdom.

beats.scene: A man sways in a tavern doorway holding an empty cup
beats.summary: Those who stay too long over wine end in poverty, trouble and sorrow.

beats.scene: A man looks over a wall at a field overgrown with thorns
beats.summary: A righteous person falls seven times and rises again, but a lazy man's field decays.

beats.scene: Scribes copy scrolls in a stone hall while King Hezekiah watches
beats.summary: The men of King Hezekiah copy out more of Solomon's proverbs, which praise searching out hidden things.

beats.scene: A silversmith lifts dark waste from a bowl of molten silver
beats.summary: As waste is taken from silver, the wicked must be taken from a king's side.

beats.scene: A guest waits at the foot of a banquet table as the host beckons
beats.summary: Do not push yourself forward before a king; it is better to be invited up.

beats.scene: A bowl of golden apples sits in a silver dish on a table
beats.summary: A word spoken at the right time is like golden apples in a setting of silver.

beats.scene: Reapers rest in a harvest field as a cool breeze blows
beats.summary: A trustworthy messenger refreshes like snow in harvest, but a boaster is like clouds without rain.

beats.scene: A man tastes a small spoon of honey beside a full honeycomb
beats.summary: Take only as much honey as you need, and do not wear out your welcome.

beats.scene: A man sings loudly to a friend who sits grieving by a fire
beats.summary: False words wound like a weapon, and cheerful songs do not suit a heavy heart.

beats.scene: A woman hands bread and water to a tired stranger at her gate
beats.summary: If your enemy is hungry, give him food, and the Lord will reward you.

beats.scene: A traveller finds a clear spring muddied by many feet
beats.summary: A righteous person who gives way to the wicked is like a muddied spring.

beats.scene: A broken city wall stands beside a traveller drinking cold water
beats.summary: Good news is like cold water, and a person without self-control is like a city with broken walls.

beats.scene: Snow falls on a hot harvest field as a farmer looks up
beats.summary: Honour does not suit a fool, just as snow does not suit summer.

beats.scene: A wise man stays silent as a loud fool argues in a market
beats.summary: Two sayings about answering a fool seem to disagree, and judgment is needed.

beats.scene: A man ties a stone into a sling and hesitates
beats.summary: Sending a message by a fool, or honouring one, is a mistake.

beats.scene: A dog returns to a scrap in a dusty yard as a man watches
beats.summary: A fool repeats his folly, but there is more hope for him than for the self-satisfied.

beats.scene: A man turns over in bed like a door on its hinges
beats.summary: The lazy person makes excuses, such as saying there is a lion in the road.

beats.scene: A woman takes the last stick from a small fire
beats.summary: Without wood a fire goes out, and without gossip a quarrel dies down.

beats.scene: A potter paints a plain clay pot with shining silver
beats.summary: Kind words from an evil heart are like silver paint on a plain pot.

beats.scene: A man looks at the morning sky and wonders about the day
beats.summary: Do not boast about tomorrow, for no one knows what a day may bring.

beats.scene: A man offers his hand to a friend with a sad face
beats.summary: Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses.

beats.scene: A blacksmith sharpens one blade against another in a glowing workshop
beats.summary: As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another.

beats.scene: One man runs from shadows at night while another stands calmly
beats.summary: The wicked run when no one chases them, but the righteous are as bold as a lion.

beats.scene: Driving rain beats down on a field of flattened crops
beats.summary: A ruler who is cruel to the poor is like rain that ruins the harvest.

beats.scene: A man kneels to confess a wrong to a friend in a quiet room
beats.summary: Whoever hides his wrongs will not prosper, but the one who confesses finds mercy.

beats.scene: A king on his throne looks coldly over a hungry crowd
beats.summary: A wicked ruler over a helpless people is like a roaring lion.

beats.scene: A man works his small field with a hoe at dawn
beats.summary: Those who work their land have plenty, but those who chase dreams grow poor.

beats.scene: A woman gives grain to a poor man at her gate
beats.summary: Honest correction wins more thanks than flattery, and whoever gives to the poor lacks nothing.

beats.scene: A crowd celebrates in a town square as an old judge passes
beats.summary: When the righteous thrive the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule they groan.

beats.scene: A calm man stands between two angry neighbours at a gate
beats.summary: A fool lets his anger out, but a wise person turns anger away.

beats.scene: A king listens to a poor farmer at the palace gate
beats.summary: A king who judges the poor with fairness will have a lasting throne.

beats.scene: A woman stands calmly before a crowd of powerful men
beats.summary: Where there is no guiding vision people lose restraint, and fear of people is a snare.

beats.scene: A man stands on a hilltop at dusk, hands raised to the sky
beats.summary: The thirtieth chapter begins with Agur, who admits his limits and asks who holds the wind.

beats.scene: A small shield leans against a stone wall beside an open scroll
beats.summary: Every word of God is true, and he is a shield to those who trust him.

beats.scene: A man in plain clothes holds a single loaf of bread in his hands
beats.summary: Agur prays for neither poverty nor riches, only for daily bread.

beats.scene: A line of proud people look down at a poor labourer
beats.summary: Agur describes a proud generation that thinks itself clean and devours the poor.

beats.scene: Cracked dry ground and a blazing fire stand beneath a dark sky
beats.summary: Some things are never satisfied: the grave, thirsty land and fire.

beats.scene: An eagle soars above a snake on a rock and a ship at sea
beats.summary: Agur lists four wonders he cannot understand.

beats.scene: A servant sits on a throne too big for him, wearing a crooked crown
beats.summary: Agur names things the earth cannot bear, such as a servant who becomes king.

beats.scene: An ant, a locust, a lizard and a rock badger sit on a rock
beats.summary: Four small creatures are called very wise: the ant, the rock badger, the locust and the lizard.

beats.scene: A lion walks proudly across a field at sunrise
beats.summary: Agur names four creatures with a stately walk, including the lion and the king.

beats.scene: A woman churns cream in a wooden churn in a bright kitchen
beats.summary: As churning cream makes butter, so stirring up anger makes strife.

beats.scene: A queen speaks quietly to her young son in a palace room
beats.summary: The last chapter opens with the words of King Lemuel, which his mother taught him.

beats.scene: A young king pushes away a cup of wine at a feast
beats.summary: Lemuel's mother warns that kings who drink may forget justice.

beats.scene: A woman stands in court beside a silent poor man, speaking for him
beats.summary: Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, and judge fairly.

beats.scene: A scribe writes the Hebrew alphabet down the side of a long scroll
beats.summary: The final poem is an alphabet poem that begins by asking who can find a capable woman.

beats.scene: A husband and wife stand together at their door in the morning
beats.summary: Her husband trusts her fully, and she brings him good all her life.

beats.scene: A woman sorts wool and flax by lamplight before dawn
beats.summary: She works with willing hands, rises in the night and feeds her household.

beats.scene: A woman plants a young vine on a sunlit hillside field
beats.summary: She considers a field, buys it and plants a vineyard from her earnings.

beats.scene: A woman spins thread by a fire while a poor visitor warms his hands
beats.summary: She spins, helps the poor and clothes her family for the snow.

beats.scene: A woman in fine linen sells folded cloth to a merchant at market
beats.summary: She makes linen and sells it, and her husband is respected at the city gate.

beats.scene: A woman laughs in the morning sun, looking out over green fields
beats.summary: She is clothed in strength and dignity, and she laughs at the days to come.

beats.scene: A woman counts jars in a lamplit pantry at the end of the day
beats.summary: She watches over her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.

beats.scene: Children and a husband stand at a table smiling at their mother
beats.summary: Her children call her blessed, and her husband says she surpasses all.

beats.scene: A young woman looks at her reflection in a still bowl of water
beats.summary: Charm is deceptive and beauty fleeting, but a woman who respects the Lord is to be praised.

beats.scene: Elders stand at the city gate to honour a woman as she approaches
beats.summary: Honour her for all her hands have done, and let her works bring her praise at the gate.

beats.scene: A teacher sets two lamps side by side, one lit and one dark
beats.summary: Looking back, the book is a book of pairs: the wise and the foolish, the honest and the false.

beats.scene: A farmer stands in a storm, hat in hand, looking at his flattened field
beats.summary: The proverbs say how life usually goes; Job and Ecclesiastes ask what to think when it does not.

beats.scene: A woman reads a small scroll by morning light at her kitchen table
beats.summary: Some readers read one chapter a day, since the book has thirty-one chapters.

beats.scene: Travellers from different lands trade sayings around a fire at night
beats.summary: Many peoples have collected wise sayings, but this book gives its own foundation for wisdom.

beats.scene: Two women, one calling in a market and one working at home
beats.summary: The book began with Wisdom as a woman and ends with a poem about a capable one.

beats.scene: A woman stands at the open door of a warm lamplit house at dusk
beats.summary: The book ends as it began: respect for the Lord, and wisdom lived out each day.

People who ignore her will call for help, but she will not answer.
But anyone who listens to Wisdom will live safely and without fear.
Look for wisdom the way a miner digs for hidden silver.
The book says that God gives wisdom and keeps good people safe.
Wisdom will help you to understand what is right, fair and good.
Wisdom also keeps you away from people who choose dark, twisted roads.
Wisdom warns the young man about people who use sweet words to trick him.

Give God the first part of your harvest, and your barns will be full.
God corrects the people he loves, as a father corrects his son.
The book says wisdom is worth more than silver, gold or jewels.
Wisdom gives a long life, and her ways are pleasant and peaceful.
God used wisdom when he made the earth and the sky.
Keep good sense, and you will walk safely and sleep well at night.
Do not hold back help from a neighbour, and never plan to hurt him.
God blesses the homes of good people, and he helps those who are humble.
A father tells his sons what his own father once taught him.
Get wisdom, even if it costs all you have, and she will honour you.
The path of good people is like morning light that grows brighter.
Guard your heart, watch your words, and look straight ahead on your road.
Sweet words can taste like honey, but later they taste bitter.
Stay far from that door, or you will lose your strength and wealth.
A husband should be faithful, like a man who drinks from his own well.
Be glad with your wife, for God sees everything that you do.
If you promised to pay a friend's debt, free yourself quickly.
Go and watch an ant, and learn how to work.
If you sleep too much, poverty will arrive like a thief.
A bad man plans evil and starts fights, so trouble will come to him.
God hates proud eyes, a lying tongue and hands that hurt the innocent.
God also hates evil plans, lying witnesses and people who start fights.
Keep your parents' teaching, because it is like a lamp on a dark road.
A man cannot carry fire in his coat and not be burned.
A hungry thief must pay back what he took, but some harm cannot be repaid.
Guard my teaching as you guard your own eyes.
One evening a father looks through his window and sees a foolish young man.
In the dark street a woman in fine clothes meets the young man.
She says that her husband is away, and she asks the young man to come in.
He follows her without thinking, like a bird that flies into a trap.
Do not follow her road, says the father, because it leads to great sorrow.
Wisdom and Folly both call from the street, but their roads are different.
Wisdom calls out from the hills and from the gates of the city.
My words are true and fair, says Wisdom, and better than silver.
Wisdom says that kings rule well when they listen to her.
Wisdom says, I love the people who love me and look for me.
Before the mountains and the seas were made, Wisdom was already there.
When God made the sky and the sea, Wisdom was there, full of joy.
Happy are the people who listen to Wisdom and wait at her door.
Wisdom has built a house, and she has set a table for guests.
A wise person is thankful when you correct him, but a mocker is angry.
Folly sits at her door and calls out to people who walk by.
A wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish son makes his mother sad.
Stolen money does not last, but doing right keeps a person safe.
Hard work brings wealth, but a lazy person sleeps through the harvest.
People remember a good person with joy, but a bad name will rot.
An honest person walks safely, but a crooked person will be found out.
Hatred stirs up trouble, but love covers every wrong.
The rich trust their wealth, but poor people have nothing to protect them.
Too many words lead to trouble, so a wise person speaks little.
When the storm has passed, the wicked are gone, but good people stand firm.
Respect for God brings a long life, and good people end in joy.
The Lord hates dishonest scales, but he is pleased by fair weights.
Pride is followed by shame, but wisdom comes with humility.
Money cannot save you on the day of trouble, but doing right can.
When good people do well, the whole city is happy.
A gossip tells secrets, but a good friend keeps them safe.
A country with no wise advisers will fall, but many advisers bring safety.
A kind woman gains honour, but a cruel man gains only money.
One person gives freely and gets richer, but another saves too much and loses.
Those who trust in money will fall, but good people grow like green leaves.
A gold ring on a pig's nose is like beauty without good sense.
A wise person loves correction, but a fool hates it.
It is better to live simply and have bread than to pretend to be great.
A good man cares for his animals, but a cruel man does not.
A fool thinks he is always right, but a wise man listens to advice.
Careless words hurt like a sword, but the words of the wise bring healing.
A kind word can cheer a heart that is heavy with worry.
Hard workers will lead, but lazy people end up working for others.
A wise child listens to his father, and careful words keep a person safe.
Wealth gained in a hurry soon shrinks, but wealth gathered slowly will grow.
Walk with the wise and you will become wise too.
A wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one pulls it down.
A clean barn has no ox, but a strong ox brings a good harvest.
There is a way that seems right, but it ends in trouble.
A patient person has great understanding, but a quick temper leads to foolish acts.
Whoever is kind to the poor honours God, who made them.
Hard work brings profit, but empty talk leads only to poverty.
Doing right makes a nation great, but wrong brings shame to any people.
A gentle answer turns away anger, but a harsh word starts a fight.
A small meal with love is better than a feast with hatred.
Plans fail without good advice, but many advisers help them to succeed.
People make their plans, but God guides their steps.
Pride comes before a fall, and a proud spirit before ruin.
A king is pleased by honest words, and his kind face gives life.
Wisdom is better than gold, and kind words are as sweet as honey.
A bad man starts fights between neighbours and leads them to do wrong.
Someone who rules his temper is better than someone who takes a city.
A dry crust with peace is better than a feast with fighting.
Starting a quarrel is like opening a hole in a dam.
A true friend loves you at all times, and a glad heart is like medicine.
Even a foolish person may seem wise if he stays quiet.
A fool does not enjoy learning, but he loves to share his own ideas.
God's name is a strong tower, and good people run to it for safety.
Answering before you listen is foolish, and it brings shame.
The first person to speak seems right, until the other person speaks too.
A friend who is hurt is harder to win back than a strong city.
Words have the power of life and death, so speak with care.
Some friends do not last, but a true friend stays closer than a brother.
It is better to be poor and honest than to be a fool.
When a person is rich, he has many friends, but the poor have few.
Be kind to the poor, because it is like lending to God.
A lazy man will not even lift his food to his mouth.
A person's plans are like deep water, but a wise person draws them out.
A good person walks with honesty, and his children are happy after him.
A buyer says the goods are bad, then goes away and boasts.
Gold and jewels are valuable, but wise words are even more rare.
The human spirit is a lamp from God that searches the heart.
God can guide a king's heart the way a farmer guides a stream.
If you ignore the poor, no one will listen to you in trouble.
It is better to live alone on a roof than with an angry person.
A good name is worth more than great riches.
Listen to the sayings of the wise, and take them to heart.
Do not rob the poor, and do not make friends with an angry man.
A person who works with great skill will serve kings.
When you eat with a ruler, take little and watch your manners.
Do not tire yourself out just to get rich.
Do not move the old stone that marks a poor family's field.
A wise child makes his parents glad, so buy truth and never sell it.
Do not envy bad people, because a house is built by wisdom.
People who drink too much wine soon end up poor and sad.
A good person who falls down seven times will get up again.
Men of King Hezekiah copied more of Solomon's sayings onto scrolls.
Take the waste out of silver, and a fine cup can be made.
Do not push yourself forward before a king, or you may be shamed.
A wise word at the right time is as lovely as golden apples.
A faithful messenger is like cool snow on a hot harvest day.
If you find honey, eat only as much as you need.
Singing happy songs to a sad person is like taking his coat in winter.
If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat.
A good person who gives in to the wicked is like a muddy spring.
A person with no self-control is like a city with broken walls.
Honour does not suit a fool, just like snow in summer.
Sometimes it is wise to answer a fool, and sometimes it is not.
Sending a message with a fool is like cutting off your own feet.
A fool does the same foolish thing again, like a dog that comes back.
A lazy man says, there is a lion in the road, so he stays home.
Without wood a fire goes out, and without gossip a quarrel ends.
Kind words from a bad heart are like silver paint on a plain pot.
Do not boast about tomorrow, because no one knows what it will bring.
Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy gives many kisses.
Iron makes iron sharp, and one friend makes another friend better.
Bad people run when no one chases them, but good people are brave.
A ruler who is cruel to the poor is like rain that ruins the crops.
Whoever admits his wrongs and stops doing them will find mercy.
A cruel ruler over poor people is like a hungry lion or bear.
Those who work their land will have plenty of food.
Whoever gives to the poor will never be in need.
When good people do well, everyone is glad, but when the wicked rule, people are unhappy.
A wise person turns away anger, but a fool lets it out.
A king who judges the poor fairly will have a lasting throne.
Fear of people is a trap, but trust in God keeps you safe.
A man named Agur asks who has held the wind in his hands.
Every word from God is true, and he protects those who trust him.
Agur asks God for enough bread, but not too little or too much.
Agur describes proud people who think they are clean and look down on others.
Some things are never full, such as fire, the grave and dry land.
Agur says that an eagle, a snake and a ship are too wonderful for him.
The earth shakes when a servant becomes a king.
Ants are small, but they are wise and store food in summer.
A lion is strong and walks proudly, and he runs from no animal.
As shaking cream makes butter, so stirring up anger makes trouble.
A king named Lemuel remembers the wise words his mother taught him.
A king should not drink too much wine, or he will forget justice.
Speak up for people who cannot speak for themselves, and judge fairly.
The last poem uses one Hebrew letter to start each line.
Her husband trusts her, and she brings him good all her life.
She gets up early, works with eager hands and feeds her family.
She buys a field and plants vines with the money she has earned.
She helps the poor, and her family is warm when it snows.
She makes fine cloth and sells it, and her husband is respected.
She is full of strength, and she can laugh at the days to come.
She watches over her house and never wastes her time.
Her children and her husband praise her and call her blessed.
Charm can fool people, and beauty fades, but respect for God is worth praise.
Give her honour for what she has done, and let the city praise her.
The book is full of pairs, such as wise and foolish, honest and false.
Proverbs says how life usually goes, but it does not promise every result.
Some readers read one chapter of Proverbs each day of the month.

B1B2: The Book of Proverbs is a collection of short sayings, and each one holds a lesson for daily life. A proverb is easy to remember, so it can be passed on from one person to the next.

The book begins by naming King Solomon, the son of David, who is remembered in the Bible for his great wisdom. However, other writers appear later in the book, and some sayings are said to have been copied out by the men of King Hezekiah.

The opening lines explain why the book was written: to help people gain wisdom and learn to live with honesty and fairness. It is meant for the young and the simple, but the wise, too, will listen and add to what they know.
The first great idea of the book is that respect for the Lord is where knowledge begins. Fools, it says, despise wisdom and refuse to be taught.
A father tells his son to listen well and never to forget his mother's teaching. Such advice, he says, will be like a beautiful crown on his head and a gold chain around his neck.

Some people will try to tempt the young man by saying, come with us, and we will wait for an innocent victim. We will fill our houses with stolen goods, they promise, and you will share one purse with us all.

Keep your feet away from their path, says the father, because they are in a hurry to do harm. It is useless to spread a net while a bird is watching, and these people are really setting a trap for themselves.

Now Wisdom herself is pictured as a woman, and she cries out in the streets, in the squares and at the city gate. How long, she asks, will the simple love being simple, and how long will mockers enjoy mocking?

Because the crowd ignored her advice, Wisdom says, she will laugh when trouble comes to them like a storm. They will call to her then, but she will not answer, for they refused to learn and must eat the fruit of their own ways.
The first chapter ends with a gentle promise of peace for the people who listen. Whoever listens to Wisdom will live in safety and will be at ease, without any dread of disaster.
The father says that wisdom is like silver hidden deep in the ground. If you listen carefully and search for understanding as hard as a miner digs, you will find it.

Then you will understand what it means to respect the Lord, says the father, because the Lord himself gives wisdom. Knowledge and understanding come from his mouth, and he is a shield to people who walk honestly.
With wisdom in your heart, you will understand what is right and fair and which path is good. Good sense will guard you, and understanding will watch over you like a guard at a gate.
Wisdom will also save you from people who speak twisted words. They leave the straight paths to walk in the dark, and they enjoy doing wrong even when it hurts others.

The father also warns about a flatterer who tempts a young man to break his promises, especially the promise of marriage. Such a road, he says, goes down toward ruin, and those who follow it seldom find their way back.
So walk in the way of good people, says the father, and keep to the paths of the honest. Those who do right will live safely in the land, but the wicked will lose it.

Do not forget my teaching, says the father, and keep my commands in your heart, because they bring long life. Let love and faithfulness never leave you, he adds, and write them on your heart, and you will win favour with God and people.

Trust the Lord with all your heart, says the writer, and do not lean on your own understanding. If you remember him in all that you do, he will make your paths straight, and respect for him will bring health to your body.
Honour the Lord with your wealth, says the book, and give him the first part of everything that you harvest. Then your barns will be full to overflowing, and your vats will burst with new wine.
My son, do not hate the Lord's correction, says the father, and do not become tired of it. The Lord corrects the people he loves, in the same way that a father corrects the son he is proud of.
Happy is the person who finds wisdom, says the book, because she is worth more than silver or gold. She is more precious than rubies, and nothing that you desire can be compared with her.

In her right hand, says the writer, Wisdom holds long life, and in her left hand she holds riches and honour. Her ways are pleasant and her paths are peaceful, and she is a tree of life to those who take hold of her.

The writer says that the Lord used wisdom when he laid the foundations of the earth. By understanding he set the heavens in place, and by knowledge the deep waters were opened and the clouds let fall the dew.

My son, keep good judgment and sound sense in view, says the father, and they will be life for your soul. Then you will walk safely on your way, and when you lie down you will not be afraid, and your sleep will be sweet.

Do not hold back good from the people who deserve it, says the father, when it is in your power to help. Never tell your neighbour to come back tomorrow when you can help today, and never plan harm against him.

The Lord's curse is on the house of the wicked, says the writer, but he blesses the home of the righteous. He laughs at proud mockers, but he gives favour to the humble, and the wise will receive honour.

Listen, my sons, to a father's teaching, says the writer, and pay attention so that you will gain understanding. When I was a boy, he says, my own father taught me to hold on to his words and so to live.

Wisdom is the first thing to seek, says the father, even if it costs everything that you own, so get understanding. Hold her close, and she will lift you up, and she will place a beautiful crown on your head.

The path of the good is like the first light of dawn, says the writer, which grows brighter until the day is full. But the way of the wicked is like deep darkness, and they do not even know what makes them fall.

Guard your heart above everything else, says the father, because the whole course of your life flows from it. Keep your speech honest, look straight ahead, and think carefully about where you put your feet.

The father says that the lips of a flatterer drip like honey, and that her words are smoother than oil. In the end, he warns, they are as bitter as a poisonous plant and as sharp as a sword that cuts both ways.

Stay far from that door, says the father, or you will give your strength to strangers and your years to the cruel. In the end you will groan and say, how I hated correction, and how I ignored the teachers who tried to help me.

Drink water from your own cistern, says the father, and running water from your own well. It is a picture of faithful love in marriage, and the water of your spring should belong to you and to no one else.
Be happy with the wife of your youth, says the father, and let her love satisfy you always. The Lord sees every path that a person takes, and the wicked will be caught in the net of their own sins.
If you have promised to pay a neighbour's debt, says the father, you are trapped by your own words. Go at once and ask to be released, and do not rest until you are free, like a bird from a trap.

Go to the ant, you lazy person, says the writer, and watch how it lives and learn from it. It has no commander, officer or ruler, yet it stores up its food in summer and gathers its harvest in the season.

How long will you lie there, asks the writer, and when will you get up from your sleep? A little sleep and a little rest, he says, and poverty will arrive like a robber and need will come like an armed man.

A troublemaker, says the book, goes about with a crooked mouth, winking with his eye and signalling with his feet and fingers. In his twisted heart he plans evil all the time and stirs up quarrels, so disaster will suddenly fall on him.
There are six things that the Lord hates, says the writer, and a seventh that is a horror to him. The first three are proud eyes, a lying tongue and hands that hurt innocent people.
The list goes on with a heart that makes wicked plans, feet that hurry to do harm and a witness who tells lies. Last comes the person who stirs up quarrels among family and neighbours.

Keep your father's command and your mother's teaching, says the writer, and tie them close to your heart. They will guide you when you walk and watch over you when you sleep, because such teaching is a lamp for your path.
Teaching like this will keep you from a flatterer's sweet words, says the father, so do not desire her beauty in your heart. Can a man carry fire in his lap, he asks, without burning his clothes?

People do not despise a thief who steals because he is hungry, says the writer, although he must pay back many times what he took. But a person who destroys another man's marriage wrecks his own life, and nothing that he can pay will satisfy the angry husband.
My son, keep my words and my commands, says the father, and you will live. Guard my teaching as you guard the apple of your eye, tie it around your fingers, and write it on the tablet of your heart.

The writer says that he once looked out through the lattice of his window and watched the street below. Among the simple people he saw a young man with no sense, who was walking toward a certain corner at dusk.

A woman came out to meet him, says the writer, dressed in fine clothes and full of cunning. She is loud and restless, and her feet never stay at home, for she waits at every corner of the streets and the squares.

She took hold of him and kissed him, and she told him that she had decorated her bed with fine linen from Egypt. Come, let us enjoy ourselves until morning, she said, for my husband is away on a long journey.
With her smooth and persuasive words she led him astray. Suddenly he followed her, like an ox walking to the slaughter or a bird flying into a net, without knowing the danger.

Now, my sons, listen to me, says the father, and do not let your heart turn toward her ways or wander onto her paths. Many have been brought down by her, he says, and her house is a road to the grave.

Both Wisdom and the flatterer call out from the street, but they lead to very different places. Some readers take the flatterer as a real woman, while others take her as a picture of Folly, the opposite of Wisdom.

Does Wisdom not call out, asks the writer, standing on the high places, at the crossroads and beside the city gates? To all of you I call, she cries, so let the simple learn good sense and let fools take it to heart.
Listen, says Wisdom, because I speak about worthy things, and my lips will say only what is right. Everything I say is true, so choose my teaching instead of silver, for I am worth more than rubies.
I live with good sense, says Wisdom, and I hate pride, arrogance and every evil way. Kings rule because of me, and rulers make fair laws, and nobles govern the earth with my help.
I love those who love me, says Wisdom, and those who look for me will find me. I offer riches and honour, and what I give is better than fine gold, and I walk in the way of what is right.

The Lord made me at the very beginning, says Wisdom, before any of his other works in the ancient past. I was there before the oceans and the springs, and before the mountains were settled in their places.

When the Lord set the skies in place and marked a circle on the face of the deep, says Wisdom, I was beside him. I was filled with delight day after day, rejoicing in his whole world and in the human race.
Now listen to me, my children, says Wisdom, because those who keep my ways are happy. Whoever finds me finds life and wins favour from the Lord, but whoever misses me harms himself.

Wisdom has built her house, says the writer, and she has carved out seven pillars to hold it up. She has prepared her food and her wine, laid her table and sent her servants to call from the highest places of the town.

If you correct a mocker, says the writer, you will only get insults, but if you correct a wise person, he will love you. Teach a wise man, and he will grow wiser, because respect for the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

Folly is loud and knows nothing, says the writer, and she sits at her door calling to people who pass by. Stolen water is sweet, she says, and secret bread tastes good, but her guests do not know that the dead are in her house.
From here the book changes its style, and the proverbs of Solomon begin as short sayings of two lines. A wise son makes his father glad, says the first, but a foolish son brings sorrow to his mother.

Treasures gained by doing wrong are of no lasting use, says the writer, but doing right can save a person's life. The Lord will not let the honest go hungry, but he will frustrate the greed of the wicked.

Lazy hands make a person poor, says the book, but hard-working hands bring wealth. The son who gathers the crops in summer is wise, but the one who sleeps through the harvest brings shame on his family.
Blessings are like a crown on the head of the righteous, says the writer. The memory of a good person is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot away.
The wise in heart accept good advice, but a foolish chatterer comes to ruin. Whoever walks honestly walks in safety, says the book, while whoever follows crooked paths will be found out.
Hatred stirs up trouble, says the writer, but love covers over every wrong. The mouth of the righteous is like a fountain of life, but violence hides behind the mouth of the wicked.
The wealth of the rich is their fortified city, says the writer, but poverty is the ruin of the poor. Whoever listens to correction is on the road to life, but whoever ignores it leads others astray.
Where there are many words, sin is never far away, says the writer, but the person who holds his tongue is wise. The tongue of the righteous is like choice silver, and their lips feed many people.
The Lord's blessing makes a person rich, says the writer, and he adds no sorrow to it. When the storm has passed, the wicked are gone, but the righteous stand firm for ever.

Respect for the Lord adds years to a life, says the book, while the years of the wicked are cut short. The hope of the righteous ends in joy, and the way of the Lord is a safe refuge for those who are honest.
The Lord hates dishonest scales, says the writer, but he is pleased by accurate weights. In a market where grain and silver were weighed by hand, a fair scale was the foundation of every deal.
When pride comes, says the writer, disgrace follows close behind, but wisdom is found with the humble. The honesty of good people guides them, while the dishonesty of the unfaithful destroys them.

Riches are of no use on the day of judgment, says the writer, but doing right can rescue a person from death. The honesty of the blameless makes their way straight, but the wicked fall through their own wickedness.

When the righteous do well, the whole city is glad, says the writer, and when the wicked die there are shouts of joy. A town is raised up by the blessing of honest people, but the words of the wicked can tear it down.
A person who has no sense laughs at his neighbour, says the writer, but a person with understanding says nothing. A gossip goes around telling secrets, but a trustworthy person keeps them safe.

Where there is no guidance, a nation falls, says the writer, but when there are many advisers, there is safety. Anyone who promises to pay a stranger's debt will suffer for it, but the one who refuses is safe.
A kind woman gains honour, says the writer, but ruthless men gain only wealth. Those who are kind do good to themselves, but the cruel bring trouble on their own heads.

One person gives freely and yet grows richer, says the writer, while another holds back too much and ends in poverty. Whoever refreshes others will be refreshed, and people curse the man who hoards grain but bless the one who sells it.

Whoever looks for good will find favour, says the writer, but evil comes to the person who goes searching for it. Those who trust in their riches will fall, but the righteous will grow like green leaves.
A beautiful woman without good sense, says the writer, is like a gold ring in a pig's nose. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and the one who wins people over is wise.
Whoever loves correction loves knowledge, says the writer, but whoever hates it is foolish. Good people win the favour of the Lord, and no one can be made safe by wickedness.

A wife of noble character is her husband's crown, says the writer, but a disgraceful one is like decay in his bones. It is better to be of no importance and have a servant than to act important and have no bread.

The righteous care about the needs of their animals, says the book, but even the kindest acts of the wicked are cruel. Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but whoever chases empty dreams has no sense.
The way of a fool seems right to him, says the writer, but a wise person listens to advice. A fool shows his anger at once, but a sensible person ignores an insult.
A truthful witness tells what is right, says the book, but a false witness tells lies. Reckless words cut like the thrust of a sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.
There is deceit in the hearts of those who plan evil, says the writer, but those who work for peace have joy. Worry weighs down the heart, but a kind word cheers it up.

Diligent hands will rule, says the writer, but the lazy will be made to work for others. The lazy person does not roast any game, but a hard-working person has riches, and in the way of righteousness there is life.

A wise child listens to his father's teaching, says the writer, but a mocker does not listen to correction. Whoever guards his lips protects his life, but whoever speaks without thinking will come to ruin.

The lazy person wants everything and gets nothing, says the writer, but the hard-working person is fully satisfied. Wealth gained in a hurry will shrink, but whoever gathers it little by little will make it grow.
Hope that is put off makes the heart sick, says the writer, but a wish that is fulfilled is a tree of life. Walk with the wise and you will become wise, but a companion of fools will suffer harm.
A wise woman builds her house, says the writer, but a foolish woman pulls it down with her own hands. Whoever lives honestly respects the Lord, but whoever walks a crooked way despises him.
Where there are no oxen, says the writer, the barn stays clean, but the strength of an ox brings in a large harvest. Stay away from a fool, because you will not hear any wise words on his lips.
There is a way that seems right to a person, says the book, but in the end it leads to death. Even in laughter the heart may ache, and joy may end in grief.
A person who is quick to anger does foolish things, says the writer, but one who is patient has great understanding. A calm heart gives life to the body, but envy makes the bones rot.
The poor are avoided even by their neighbours, says the writer, but the rich have many friends. Whoever is unkind to the poor insults their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honours God.
All hard work brings a profit, says the writer, but mere talk leads only to poverty. A truthful witness saves lives, but a false witness tells nothing but lies.
Righteousness lifts up a nation, says the writer, but sin is a disgrace to any people. A king is pleased with a wise servant, but he is angry with one who brings him shame.
A gentle answer turns away anger, says the writer, but a harsh word stirs it up. The tongue of the wise makes knowledge attractive, but the mouth of fools pours out folly.
The eyes of the Lord are in every place, says the writer, and a happy heart makes a cheerful face. Better a dish of vegetables with love, he says, than a fattened calf with hatred.
Plans fail for lack of advice, says the writer, but they succeed when there are many advisers. A person finds joy in giving a fitting answer, and how good a timely word can be!

Commit your work to the Lord, says the writer, and your plans will succeed, for the Lord weighs the motives behind them. People make their plans in their hearts, but it is the Lord who directs their steps.
Pride goes before destruction, says the writer, and a proud spirit before a fall. It is better to be humble and poor than to share the loot with the proud.

A king delights in honest lips, says the writer, and he loves the person who speaks what is right. A king's anger is dangerous, but a wise person can calm it, and his favour is like a rain cloud in spring.
How much better it is to get wisdom than gold, says the writer, and to choose understanding rather than silver. Pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the body.

A troublemaker plots evil, says the writer, and his words are like a scorching fire. He stirs up quarrels, he separates close friends with gossip, and he leads his neighbour down a path that is not good.

Grey hair is a crown of splendour, says the writer, when it is found on a person who has lived rightly. Someone who is patient is better than a warrior, and someone who rules his temper is better than someone who captures a city.
A dry crust of bread with peace is better than a house full of feasting with quarrelling, says the writer. Grandchildren are the crown of the old, and parents are the pride of their children.

Starting a quarrel is like breaking open a dam, says the writer, so drop the matter before a dispute begins. Whoever forgives an offence promotes love, but whoever keeps repeating it separates close friends.
A friend loves at all times, says the writer, and a brother is born to help in time of trouble. A cheerful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.

A person with understanding keeps wisdom in sight, says the writer, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth. Even a fool seems wise if he stays quiet, and the one who holds back his words seems sensible.

A person who stays apart from others looks only for what he wants, says the writer, and he quarrels with all good sense. A fool takes no pleasure in understanding, but only in telling people what he thinks.
The name of the Lord is a strong tower, says the writer, and the righteous run into it and are safe. The rich, by contrast, imagine that their wealth is a high wall around a fortified city.
Before a person's downfall the heart is proud, says the writer, but humility comes before honour. To answer a question before you have listened to it is foolish, and it brings shame.

A person's spirit can carry him through sickness, says the writer, but who can bear a spirit that is crushed? The first person to tell his story seems right, until someone else comes forward and asks questions.

Casting lots settles disputes and keeps strong opponents apart, says the writer. A brother who has been wronged is harder to win back than a fortified city, and quarrels are like the bars of a castle.
The tongue has the power of life and death, says the writer, and those who love to talk will eat what it grows. Whoever finds a wife finds something good and receives favour from the Lord.
The poor person pleads for mercy, says the writer, but the rich person answers harshly. Some friends do not last, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.
It is better to be poor and honest, says the writer, than to be a fool who speaks crooked words. Wanting something without knowledge is not good, and whoever hurries too fast will miss the way.
Wealth brings many friends, says the writer, but a poor person is left alone even by his friend. Many people try to win the favour of a ruler, and everyone is a friend of the one who gives gifts.
It is to a person's glory to overlook an offence, and whoever is kind to the poor is lending to the Lord. Many plans are in a person's heart, but it is the Lord's purpose that will stand.

The lazy person buries his hand in the dish, says the writer, and will not even lift it back to his mouth. Wine makes a person foolish and strong drink makes him noisy, and whoever is led astray by them is not wise.
The purposes in a person's heart are like deep water, says the writer, but a person with insight can draw them out. Avoiding a quarrel is honourable, though every fool is quick to start one.
Many people claim to have unfailing love, says the writer, but who can find someone who is truly trustworthy? The righteous walk in honesty, and their children are happy after them.
It is no good, says the buyer, but then he goes away and boasts about his bargain. Bread gained by cheating tastes sweet, but in the end the mouth is full of gravel.

There is gold and there are many rubies, says the writer, but lips that speak knowledge are a rare jewel. Do not say, I will pay you back for this wrong, because it is better to wait for the Lord to help you.
The human spirit is the lamp of the Lord, says the writer, and it searches every part of a person's heart. The glory of the young is their strength, and the splendour of the old is their grey hair.
The heart of a king is like a stream of water in the Lord's hand, and he turns it wherever he pleases. To do what is right and just is more pleasing to the Lord than sacrifice.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, says the writer, will cry out one day and not be answered. The plans of the diligent lead to profit, but everyone who is in a hurry comes to poverty.
It is better to live in a corner of the roof, says the writer, than to share a house with a quarrelling person. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but victory belongs to the Lord.
A good name is worth more than great riches, says the writer, and favour is better than silver or gold. Teach a child the way he should go, and even when he is old he will not leave it.
Pay attention, says the writer, and listen to the sayings of the wise, and take my teaching to heart. I am teaching you today, even you, so that your trust may be in the Lord.
Do not rob the poor because they are poor, says the writer, and do not crush the needy in court. The Lord will take up their case, and you should not make friends with a person who is quick to anger.

Do not promise to pay another person's debt, says the writer, or even your bed may be taken from you. A person who is skilled in his work, he adds, will serve before kings and not before ordinary people.
When you sit down to eat with a ruler, says the writer, notice carefully what is in front of you. Do not crave his fine food, because it may be a trick, and do not eat the bread of a mean host.
Do not wear yourself out to get rich, says the writer, and be wise enough to stop. Riches can vanish in a moment, as if they had grown wings and flown away like an eagle.
Do not move an ancient boundary stone, says the writer, or take over the fields of orphans. Their Defender is strong, and he will take up their case against you.
My son, if your heart is wise, says the father, then my own heart will be glad. Listen to your father, and do not despise your mother when she is old, but buy the truth and never sell it.

Do not envy sinners in your heart, says the writer, but continue to respect the Lord, for there is a hope for the future. Do not envy evil people or wish to be with them, because their hearts plan violence, but a house is built by wisdom.

Do not join those who drink too much wine, says the writer, for drunkards become poor and sleepiness dresses a person in rags. Who has trouble, who has sorrow and who has quarrels, he asks, if not those who stay too long over their wine?

A good person may fall seven times, says the writer, but he gets up again, while the wicked stumble when trouble comes. Do not be glad when your enemy falls, and do not let your heart rejoice when he stumbles.
These are more proverbs of Solomon, says the writer, which the men of King Hezekiah of Judah copied out. It is the glory of God to hide a matter, but it is the glory of kings to search it out.
Take the waste out of silver, says the writer, and a silversmith can make a fine cup. In the same way, take the wicked away from a king, and his throne will be made firm by justice.
Do not push yourself forward in front of the king, says the writer, or take a place among the great. It is better to hear the words, come up here, than to be put lower in front of a noble.
A word that is spoken at the right time, says the writer, is like golden apples in a setting of silver. A wise rebuke is like a gold earring to an ear that is willing to listen.
A trustworthy messenger is as refreshing as snow in the heat of harvest, says the writer. A person who boasts of gifts he never gives is like clouds and wind that bring no rain.

If you find honey, says the writer, eat only as much as you need, or you will have too much and be sick. Do not visit your neighbour's house too often, or he will grow tired of you and come to hate you.

A person who tells lies about his neighbour, says the writer, is like a club, a sword or a sharp arrow. Trusting an unfaithful person in a time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that cannot walk.
If your enemy is hungry, says the writer, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. You will heap burning coals on his head, and the Lord will reward you.
The north wind brings rain, says the writer, and a sly tongue brings angry looks. When a righteous person gives way before the wicked, it is like a muddy spring or a polluted well.
Good news from a far country, says the writer, is like cold water to a thirsty soul. A person without self-control is like a city whose walls have been broken down.

Honour does not suit a fool, says the writer, any more than snow in summer or rain at harvest. A curse that has no cause does not land on its target, but flutters away like a sparrow or a swallow in flight.

One verse says not to answer a fool by his own foolish ways, or you will become like him. The very next verse says to answer a fool in just that way, and a wise person must decide which advice fits the moment.

Sending a message by the hand of a fool, says the writer, is like cutting off your own feet and asking for trouble. A wise saying in the mouth of a fool is as useless as the legs of a person who cannot walk.
A fool repeats his folly, says the writer, as a dog goes back to what it has left on the ground. There is more hope for a fool than for a person who is wise in his own eyes.
The lazy person says, there is a lion in the road, so he stays at home. As a door turns on its hinges, so he turns over in bed, and thinks he is wiser than seven sensible people.

Without wood a fire goes out, says the writer, and where there is no gossip a quarrel dies down. As charcoal keeps embers glowing and wood keeps a fire alive, so a quarrelsome person keeps a dispute going.
Warm words from an evil heart, says the writer, are like silver paint on a plain clay pot. The person who hates may hide it with kind words, but inside he is full of lies.
Do not boast about tomorrow, says the writer, because you do not know what a day may bring. Let someone else praise you, and not your own mouth, a stranger and not your own lips.
Wounds from a friend can be trusted, says the writer, but an enemy multiplies kisses. Perfume and incense bring joy to the heart, and so does the sweetness of a friend's advice.

As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another, and as water shows a face, so the heart shows the person. Know well the condition of your flocks, says the writer, because riches do not last for ever.
The wicked run away when no one is chasing them, says the writer, but the righteous are as bold as a lion. When a land is in revolt it has many rulers, but one wise ruler can bring order.
A ruler who is cruel to the poor, says the writer, is like a driving rain that leaves no crops. It is better to be a poor person who lives honestly than a rich person whose ways are crooked.

Whoever hides his wrongs will not do well, says the writer, but the one who admits them and gives them up will find mercy. When the righteous win, there is great joy, but when the wicked rise, people hide.

A wicked ruler over a helpless people, says the writer, is like a roaring lion or a charging bear. A ruler who hates dishonest gain will reign for a long time, but one who lacks judgment is a cruel tyrant.

Whoever works his land will have plenty of food, says the writer, but whoever chases empty dreams will have plenty of poverty. A faithful person will be richly blessed, but whoever is eager to get rich will not go unpunished.

In the end, says the writer, a person who gives honest correction will win more thanks than one who flatters. Whoever gives to the poor will lack nothing, but whoever closes his eyes to them will receive many curses.

When the righteous do well, says the writer, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan. By justice a king makes a country strong, but the person who is greedy for bribes brings it down.
A person who flatters his neighbour, says the writer, is spreading a net for his feet. A fool lets out all his anger at once, but a wise person keeps himself calm and turns anger away.
