If a king judges the poor with fairness, says the writer, his throne will be secure for ever. The poor person and the oppressor have this in common, that the Lord gives light to the eyes of both.

Where there is no guiding vision, says the writer, the people lose all restraint, but blessed is the one who keeps the teaching. Fear of other people is a trap, but whoever trusts in the Lord is kept safe.

These are the words of Agur, son of Jakeh, who begins by saying that he is tired and that he has not learned wisdom. Who has gone up to heaven and come down, he asks, and who has gathered the wind in his hands?
Every word of God is true, says Agur, and he is a shield to those who take refuge in him. Do not add anything to his words, or he will correct you and prove you wrong.

Agur makes a short prayer with two requests: to keep lies far from him, and to have neither poverty nor riches. Give me only the food that I need each day, he asks, so that I do not grow proud or turn to stealing.
Agur describes a generation that is pure in its own eyes, though it has not been washed of its dirt. Its eyes are proud, and its teeth are like swords that eat up the poor and the needy.
There are things that are never satisfied, says Agur, and they never say enough. They are the grave, the land that is always thirsty for water, and the fire that burns on.
Agur says that three things are too wonderful for him, and four he cannot understand. The list is an eagle in flight, a snake on a rock, a ship at sea and a man's way with a young woman.
Under three things the earth shakes, says Agur, and under four it cannot bear the weight. Among them are a servant who becomes king and a fool who has more than enough to eat.
Four things on earth are small, says Agur, yet they are very wise. Ants are not strong, but they store their food in summer, and locusts have no king, yet they all move forward together in ranks.
Three things walk with a stately step, says Agur, and four move with pride. A lion, the strongest of animals, turns back from nothing, and a king is safe when no one rises against him.
If you have played the fool by boasting, or if you have planned something evil, says Agur, put your hand over your mouth. As churning cream makes butter, so stirring up anger makes trouble.
The last chapter begins with the words of King Lemuel, which his mother taught him. Listen, my son, she says, the son I prayed for, and do not give your strength to things that ruin kings.
It is not for kings to drink wine, says Lemuel's mother, or for rulers to want strong drink. If they drink, they may forget what the law says and take away the rights of people who are suffering.
Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, says the queen mother, and for the rights of all who have nothing. Speak up and judge fairly, and defend the rights of the poor and the needy.

The last poem of the book is an alphabet poem, and in Hebrew each line begins with the next letter of the alphabet. It begins with a question, who can find a capable wife, and the answer is that she is worth far more than rubies.
Her husband trusts her completely, says the poem, and he never lacks anything of value. She brings him good and not harm, all the days of her life.
She chooses wool and flax and works with willing hands, says the poem. She gets up while it is still night to give food to her family and to her servants.
She looks at a field and buys it, says the poem, and with the money she has earned she plants a vineyard. Her arms are strong for the work, and her lamp does not go out at night.

Her hands hold the spindle, says the poem, and yet she opens her hand to the poor and reaches out to the needy. When it snows she has no fear for her family, because all of them are dressed in warm scarlet clothes.

She makes coverings for her bed and wears fine linen, says the poem, and she sells linen garments to the merchants. Her husband is respected at the city gate, where he takes his seat among the elders of the land.
She is clothed with strength and dignity, says the poem, and she can laugh at the days to come. She speaks with wisdom, and faithful teaching is always on her tongue.

She watches over everything that happens in her household, says the poem, and she never eats the bread of idleness. Many readers see the poem as praise for steady care and hard work that makes a home a good place.
Her children rise up and call her blessed, says the poem, and her husband also praises her. Many women do noble things, he says, but you are better than them all.
Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, says the poem, but a woman who respects the Lord should be praised. The poem does not say that looks are wrong, only that they do not last.
Honour her for all that her hands have done, says the poem, and let her works bring her praise at the city gate. The gate was where elders met and judged, so this praise is public and well earned.
The book is full of pairs: the wise and the foolish, the honest and the false, the lazy and the hard-working. Each pair is like two roads, and the book asks the reader which one he will take.
The proverbs say how life usually goes, not how it must go every time. Other books of the Hebrew Bible, such as Job and Ecclesiastes, ask what we should think when life does not follow the rule.
Some readers read one chapter of Proverbs on each day of the month, because the book has thirty-one chapters. In this way a few sayings a day can become a habit of reflection over a lifetime.

People in many lands have collected wise sayings, and some of the sayings in this book are like ones found in other nations. Even so, the book gives its own reason for wisdom, which is respect for the Lord.

The book began with Wisdom as a woman who calls in the streets, and it ends with a poem about a capable woman. Many readers see the poem both as a portrait of a real woman and as a picture of Wisdom at home.
So the book ends as it began, with respect for the Lord and with wisdom shown in daily work. A saying is only words until someone lives it, and the best proof of wisdom is an ordinary day lived well.
C1C2: The Book of Proverbs is built from short sayings, each of which packs a lesson about daily life into a line or two that is easy to remember. The Hebrew word for such a saying can also mean a comparison, and many of the sayings work by setting two pictures side by side. Behind them stands a simple belief, that living well is a skill as well as a matter of rules, and that this skill can be learned.

Tradition connects the book with Solomon, the son of David, who the Hebrew Bible says asked God for wisdom and became famous for it far beyond Israel. Yet the book names other voices as well, among them Agur and the mother of King Lemuel, and it says that the men of King Hezekiah copied out a further group of sayings. Most scholars therefore think that the collection grew over several centuries, gathered and arranged by many hands.

In its opening lines the book states its purpose plainly, which is to teach wisdom and discipline, to help readers grasp deep sayings and to guide them toward what is right, just and fair. The simple are promised good sense, and the young are promised knowledge and the habit of thinking ahead. Even the wise, it adds, will listen and grow in learning, for no one in this book is ever too old to be taught.

The motto of the whole book appears at the very start, where it says that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge. Most readers understand the word fear here as awe and deep respect, not as terror, so that wisdom begins when a person admits that there is a power greater than himself. Fools, the verse goes on, despise wisdom and instruction, and the rest of the book can be read as a long invitation not to be one of them.

Here a father begins the long address that fills the first nine chapters, urging his son to listen to his instruction and never to put aside his mother's teaching. Such guidance, he promises, will sit upon the young man like a graceful garland on his head and a chain of gold around his neck. The picture is of wisdom as an ornament, something handed down in a family and worn with quiet pride.

Next the father warns his son about a gang that will invite him to join them, saying, come with us, let us lie in wait for the innocent and take whatever we please. They promise that their houses will be filled with stolen goods and that the newcomer will share one purse with all of them. It is a temptation that sounds like friendship and loyalty, and that is exactly why the father thinks it must be named.

Do not walk with them, the father insists, for their feet hurry toward harm, and the ambush that they prepare is in truth laid for themselves. He adds a little proverb about birds, saying that it is pointless to spread a net while the bird is watching, so the schemers are blind to the trap they are building. Greed, he concludes, takes away the life of everyone who yields to it, however clever the plan may seem.

In a famous passage Wisdom is pictured as a woman who will not wait quietly in a school or temple but cries out in the streets, the open squares and the busy city gates. How long, she asks, will the simple go on loving their simple ways, the mockers delight in mocking and the fools hate knowledge? If they will only turn at her warning, she promises to pour out her thoughts to them and to make her words known.

Wisdom warns that those who ignored her calls will one day meet disaster, which will sweep over them like a storm and leave them in distress. Then they will cry out to her, but she will not answer, because they hated knowledge and chose not to respect the Lord. They will eat the fruit of their own ways, the passage says, and be filled with their own schemes.

The chapter closes on a note of reassurance, so that the stern warning is not the last word. Whoever listens to Wisdom, she says, will live in safety and will be at ease, without any dread of disaster. The first nine chapters will return to this choice again and again, as a father shows his son the two roads and begs him to take the better one.

The father begins the second chapter with a long sentence of conditions, saying that if his son will accept his words, treasure his commands and call out for understanding, then something wonderful will follow. He asks the young man to search for wisdom as he would search for silver, and to dig for it as a miner digs for buried treasure. The picture teaches that wisdom is not found by chance but by patient, hopeful labour.

Then, the father says, you will understand what it means to respect the Lord and you will find the knowledge of God. It is the Lord himself who gives wisdom, and from his mouth come knowledge and understanding, though the reader is asked to do the digging. He stores up success for the honest and is a shield to those who walk without blame, guarding the paths of the just and watching over those who are faithful to him.

With wisdom, the father promises, you will understand what is right and just and fair, and you will see every good path that is open to you. Wisdom will enter your heart and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul, as welcome as a guest who has come in from the cold. Good judgment will watch over you, and understanding will guard you, so that you are protected by your own good sense.

Wisdom will also rescue you, the father says, from the ways of wicked men whose words are twisted and whose speech cannot be trusted. Such people leave the straight paths to walk in dark ways, and they take pleasure in doing wrong and rejoice in the crookedness of evil. Their roads wind in every direction but never lead to anything good, and the traveller who follows them is soon lost.

The father then warns his son of a second danger, a smooth-tongued person who has abandoned her faithfulness and who tempts the young to do the same. The passage is about the promise of marriage and the harm that comes when it is broken, and it says that such a road sinks toward death. Readers have long understood the warning in a wider way, as a caution to anyone who is led astray by flattery.

The conclusion is that the young man should walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous. Those who are upright, the father promises, will live in the land and remain in it, while the wicked will be cut off from it and the unfaithful torn away. In ancient Israel, where a family lived by the land, there was hardly a stronger image of safety and belonging.

At the start of the third chapter the father says, my son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commands. They will add length of days and years of peace to your life, and he asks that love and faithfulness never leave his son. Bind them around your neck, he says, and write them on the tablet of your heart, and you will win favour and a good name in the eyes of God and of people.

This is one of the best-known passages in the whole book, and it says, trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, the writer says, and he will make your paths straight. The father adds that one should not be wise in his own eyes but should respect the Lord and turn from evil, which, in the book's poetic language, will bring health to the body and refreshment to the bones.

Honour the Lord with your wealth, the book says, and with the first and best part of everything that you harvest. In the farming world of ancient Israel, to give the first fruits of the crop was a way of admitting that the harvest was a gift and not merely a reward. Then, the writer promises, your barns will be filled to overflowing and your vats will burst with new wine, though many readers take this promise as a hopeful picture and not a guarantee.

The father asks his son not to despise the Lord's discipline or to resent his rebuke, because the Lord corrects those whom he loves. He compares this to a father who corrects the son in whom he delights, so that the correction is a sign of care and not of rejection. It is a hard lesson to learn at any age, and the book returns to it often, saying that the person who welcomes correction is the person who grows.

Blessed is the person who finds wisdom, the writer says, and the one who gains understanding, for she is a better investment than silver and a better return than fine gold. She is more precious than rubies, and nothing that a person might wish for can be set beside her. The comparison is deliberate, because the book wants its readers to see that the things they chase are cheap beside the thing that they are likely to ignore.

In her right hand, the poem says, Wisdom holds long life, and in her left hand she holds riches and honour, as if she were offering gifts to those who come to her. Her ways are pleasant ways, and all her paths are peace, so that the wise life is pictured as a road worth walking for its own sake. To those who take hold of her she is a tree of life, and whoever holds her fast is called happy.

The writer then lifts his eyes from the village to the whole creation, saying that by wisdom the Lord founded the earth and by understanding he set the heavens in their place. By his knowledge the deep waters were broken open and the clouds let fall the dew, which is the language of a farmer who sees order in everything that grows. The suggestion is that wisdom is not only a human skill but is written into the structure of the world, and that a person who lives wisely is living with the grain of things.

My son, the father says, do not let good judgment and sound sense out of your sight, for they will be life to your soul and an ornament for your neck. Then you will go on your way in safety, and your foot will not stumble, and when you lie down you will not be afraid. Your sleep will be sweet, and you need not fear sudden disaster, for the Lord will be at your side and will keep your foot from the snare.

Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, the father says, when it is in your power to act, and do not tell your neighbour to come back tomorrow if you have it with you today. He adds that you should never plot harm against someone who lives nearby and trusts you, nor pick a quarrel for no reason when he has done you no wrong. Do not envy a violent person or copy his ways, he concludes, for the Lord detests the crooked but takes the honest into his confidence.

The Lord's curse is on the house of the wicked, the passage says, but he blesses the home of the righteous, and the point is that character decides what a house is worth, however grand it looks. He mocks those who mock him, but he gives grace to the humble, which is an idea that returns in many later writings. The wise will inherit honour, the writer says, while fools will find that they have won nothing but shame.

In the fourth chapter the father steps back and tells his son where his own wisdom came from, and the reader learns that it was handed down through the generations. Listen, he says, to a father's instruction, for I too was once a son, young and tender and my mother's only child, and my father taught me to hold fast to his words. Keep my commands, he told me, and you will live, and so the father passes on to his son what was given to him.

Get wisdom, the father says, and get understanding, and do not forget my words or turn away from them. Do not abandon her, and she will keep you safe, so love her, and she will watch over you, and though it cost all that you have, get understanding. Prize her, and she will lift you high, he promises, and she will honour you if you embrace her, and place on your head a garland of grace and a crown of splendour.

The path of the righteous, the writer says, is like the first gleam of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until the full light of day. The way of the wicked, by contrast, is like deep darkness, and they do not know what makes them stumble, which may be the most frightening image in the passage. The father urges his son to avoid that path altogether, not to set foot on it and not even to walk near it, but to turn from it and pass on.

Above all else, guard your heart, the father tells his son, for everything that you do flows from it, like water from a spring. Put away crooked speech, he says, and keep corrupt talk far from your lips, and let your eyes look straight ahead and your gaze be fixed before you. Give careful thought to the paths for your feet and be steadfast in all your ways, and do not swerve to the right or to the left, but keep your foot from evil.

The father opens the fifth chapter by asking his son to listen closely to his wisdom, because the lips of a flatterer drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil. The sweetness does not last, he warns, for in the end she is as bitter as a poisonous plant and as sharp as a sword that cuts on both edges. The passage is a warning about temptation to unfaithfulness, and its lesson is that what is pleasant to the tongue at the start may be ruinous in the end.

Keep your way far from her, the father says, and do not go near the door of her house, or you will hand your strength to others and your years to someone cruel. Strangers will feast on your wealth, he adds, and the fruit of your labour will enrich another man's household. At the end of your life you will groan, and you will say, how I hated discipline, and how my heart despised correction, and the sorrow in those words is the sorrow of a person who learned too late.

Drink water from your own cistern, the father says, and running water from your own well, which is a picture of faithful love in marriage. Water was precious in a dry land, and a well that belonged to a household was a treasure to be guarded and enjoyed with thanks. Should your springs overflow into the streets, he asks, and then he answers his own question, saying that they should be yours alone and not shared with strangers.

May your fountain be blessed, the father says, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth, as lovely and graceful as a deer. Let her love satisfy you at all times, he says, and why should you, my son, be carried away by the charms of someone else? For your ways are in full view of the Lord, who weighs all your paths, and the wicked are trapped in the net of their own sins and die for want of discipline.

If you have put up security for your neighbour, the writer says, and have shaken hands on a pledge for a stranger, then you have been trapped by what you said. The remedy, he adds, is to act at once, to humble yourself and press your neighbour to release you, and to give your eyes no sleep until you are free. Save yourself like a gazelle from the hunter, he says, and like a bird from the snare of the fowler, which suggests that a debt promised in haste is a danger that can be escaped only by speed.

Go to the ant, you who are lazy, the writer says, and consider its ways and be wise. It has no commander and no overseer and no ruler, and yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest, quietly doing the work that needs to be done. The little insect is a teacher who never speaks, and the reader is invited to admire a creature that needs no one to tell it what the season requires.

How long will you lie there, the writer asks the lazy one, and when will you get up from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, he says, and poverty will come on you like a robber and scarcity like an armed man. The warning is not against rest but against the habit of putting things off, which steals so gently that its victim hardly notices that anything has gone.

A troublemaker and a villain, the book says, is someone who goes about with a crooked mouth, winking with his eye and signalling with his feet and pointing with his fingers. His heart is twisted and he plans evil all the time, and he spreads quarrels wherever he goes, like a man scattering seeds of discord. Therefore disaster will overtake him in an instant, the writer says, and he will be broken suddenly, and no one will be able to mend him.

There are six things that the Lord hates, the writer says, and seven that are a horror to him, using a pattern of numbers that is common in the poetry of the ancient world. The list opens with haughty eyes, then a lying tongue, and then hands that shed innocent blood, so that the first three describe pride, deceit and violence. The reader senses that these are not small faults but the three things that most quickly poison a community.

The list continues with a heart that devises wicked plans, feet that are quick to rush into evil, and a false witness who pours out lies. The seventh and last item is a person who stirs up conflict among others, who is perhaps the most subtle of the troublemakers, since he rarely does any harm with his own hands. Together the seven show that, for the writer, wrongdoing begins in the eyes, the heart and the tongue long before it reaches the hands.

Keep your father's command, the writer says, and do not forsake your mother's teaching, but bind them upon your heart always and fasten them around your neck. When you walk, they will guide you, and when you sleep, they will watch over you, and when you wake, they will speak to you. For the command is a lamp, he adds, and the teaching is a light, and the corrections of discipline are the way to life.

Such teaching will keep you from the smooth tongue of a flatterer, the father says, so do not desire her beauty in your heart or let her glances capture you. He then asks two questions that need no answer, which are whether a man can scoop fire into his lap without burning his clothes, and whether he can walk on hot coals without scorching his feet. The point is that some mistakes cannot be played with, and that the cost of a moment's pleasure may fall on a whole life.

People do not despise a thief who steals to satisfy his hunger, the writer observes, yet when he is caught he must pay back sevenfold, even if it costs him everything in his house. By contrast, the person who destroys another man's marriage has no sense at all, for he destroys himself and earns wounds and disgrace that cannot be wiped away. The husband's jealousy will be furious, the writer adds, and he will accept no payment and no gift, which means that some harm is beyond the reach of any repayment.

My son, keep my words and store up my commands within you, the father says, and keep my commands and you will live. Guard my teaching as the apple of your eye, he continues, using an old picture for the pupil, which a person protects without thinking, and bind it on your fingers and write it on the tablet of your heart. Call wisdom your sister, he adds, and call understanding your close friend, so that these two companions may keep you from the stranger with her smooth words.

The writer now tells a story from his own window, saying that he looked out through the lattice of his house and saw among the simple ones a young man who had no sense. The youth was crossing the street near her corner and walking in the direction of her house, in the twilight, in the evening, as the night grew black and dark. The scene is told like a short film, with a watching narrator who sees the danger long before the young man does.

Then a woman came out to meet him, the writer says, dressed for the occasion and full of secret plans, and the details of her character are quickly sketched. She is loud and defiant, he says, and her feet never stay at home, for now she is in the street, now in the squares, lurking at every corner. She took hold of him and kissed him, and with a bold face she spoke to him, so that everything about her seemed to be calculated to catch a young man off guard.

She told him that she had spread her bed with coloured linens from Egypt and perfumed it with myrrh, aloes and cinnamon, which are the luxuries of the story. Come, she said, let us drink deeply of love until morning, for my husband is not at home, and he has gone on a long journey and has taken a bag of money with him. Her speech is full of reassurance, and that is just the thing that makes it dangerous, for every difficulty has been explained away before the young man can raise it.

With persuasive words she led him astray, the writer says, and with smooth talk she compelled him, and all at once he followed her. He went like an ox going to the slaughter, like a deer walking into a noose, like a bird darting into a snare, and he did not know that it would cost him his life. The three pictures rise one above another, and each shows an animal that sees only the bait and never the trap behind it.

Now then, my sons, listen to me, the father says, and pay attention to what I say, and do not let your heart turn aside to her ways or stray into her paths. Many are the victims she has brought down, he adds, and her slain are a mighty throng, and her house is a highway to the grave, leading down to the chambers of death. Whatever the details of the story, the teaching is plain, which is that a pleasant road may end somewhere the traveller would never have chosen.

The reader will have noticed that this woman and Wisdom, whom the book has pictured in the previous chapters, are in many ways each other's opposite, since both stand in the street and both call out to the simple. One offers life and the other the grave, and the difference lies in where each of them leads, which the traveller cannot see at the start. Some readers understand the flatterer as a real person who tempts the young, while others take her as a poetic picture of Folly, and the book is wise enough to allow both readings at once.

The eighth chapter opens with a question, which is whether Wisdom does not call and Understanding does not raise her voice. On the heights beside the road, where the paths meet, and beside the gates leading into the city, she cries aloud to all who come and go. To you, people, I call out, she says, and you who are simple, gain prudence, and you who are foolish, set your hearts on it.

Listen, Wisdom says, for I have worthy things to say, and my lips will speak what is right, since my mouth speaks the truth and wickedness is detestable to my lips. All the words of my mouth are just, and none of them is crooked or twisted, and to those who understand they are all plain. Choose my instruction instead of silver and knowledge rather than choice gold, she says, for wisdom is more precious than rubies, and nothing that you desire can compare with her.

I, Wisdom, live together with prudence, the speaker says, and I possess knowledge and good judgment, and to respect the Lord is to hate evil, so I hate pride and arrogance and crooked talk. Counsel and sound judgment are mine, she adds, and I have understanding and strength, and by me kings reign and rulers make laws that are just. By me princes govern and all nobles who rule on the earth, a claim that suggests that even the powerful need teaching and that a nation is only as good as the wisdom of its leaders.

I love those who love me, Wisdom says, and those who seek me find me, which is one of the most hopeful promises in the book. With me are riches and honour, enduring wealth and prosperity, and what I give is better than fine gold, and what I yield is choicer than silver. I walk in the way of righteousness, along the paths of justice, she adds, and I give a rich inheritance to those who love me and fill their treasuries.

In the best-known part of the chapter, Wisdom speaks of her origin, saying that the Lord brought her forth as the first of his works, before his deeds of old. She was formed long ages ago, at the very beginning, before the world began, before there were any oceans or any springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place and before the hills she was given birth, and by that point the poem has made Wisdom older than everything that can be seen.

When the Lord set the heavens in place, Wisdom says, I was there, as he marked out the horizon on the face of the deep and fixed the fountains of the deep. When he gave the sea its limit so that the waters would not overstep his command, and when he marked out the foundations of the earth, I was there beside him. The Hebrew word for her place there is hard to translate, and some read it as a craftsman and others as a child, but all agree that she delighted in the Lord's world.

Now then, my children, listen to me, says Wisdom, for blessed are those who keep my ways. Listen to my instruction and be wise, she says, and do not ignore it, for blessed is the person who listens to me, watching daily at my doors and waiting beside my doorway. Whoever finds me finds life and receives favour from the Lord, but whoever fails to find me harms himself, and all who hate me, she concludes, are in love with death.

The ninth chapter turns from a speech to a picture, saying that Wisdom has built her house and has hewn out its seven pillars. She has prepared her meat and mixed her wine and set her table, and she has sent out her servants to call from the highest point of the city. Let all who are simple come in here, she says, and come, eat my food and drink the wine that I have mixed, and leave your simple ways and you will live, and walk in the way of understanding.

Whoever corrects a mocker, the writer says, only earns insults, and whoever rebukes a wicked person earns abuse, so do not rebuke a mocker or he will hate you. Rebuke a wise person, and he will love you, and instruct a wise person, and he will be wiser still, for a good teacher is a gift to the wise and a trouble to the scornful. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, the passage repeats, and if you are wise your wisdom will reward you, but if you are a mocker you alone will bear the cost.

In the last scene of the first section the book sets a second woman beside the first, saying that the woman Folly is loud and undisciplined and knows nothing at all. She sits at the door of her house, on a seat at the highest point of the city, and she calls to those who pass by and go straight on their way, saying that whoever is simple should come in. Stolen water is sweet, she says, and food eaten in secret is delicious, but her guests do not know that the dead are there and that they are in the depths of the grave.

From the tenth chapter the style of the book changes, and the proverbs of Solomon begin as a long run of short sayings, each of two lines and each complete in itself. The first sets a wise son beside a foolish one, saying that the wise son brings joy to his father, while the foolish son is a grief to his mother. The sayings are not arranged like an argument but are scattered like seeds, and the reader is invited to pick them up one at a time and carry each of them away.

Ill-gotten treasures have no lasting value, the writer says, but righteousness delivers from death, and the point is that wealth gained by wrong does not give its owner any security. The Lord does not let the righteous go hungry, he continues, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked, so that honest people have good reason to hope. The saying does not promise that no honest person will ever know hunger, and most readers take it as a statement of the way the world is meant to work, and of the faith of the writer.

Lazy hands make for poverty, the book says, but diligent hands bring wealth, and the author does not soften the contrast. The son who gathers the crops in summer is wise, but the one who sleeps during the harvest is a disgrace, for the harvest was a short season when a whole family's year was decided. A farmer in the ancient hills knew that there were days on which sleep was a luxury that nobody could afford, and the saying would have been obvious to those who first heard it.

Blessings are a crown on the head of the righteous, the writer says, but violence overwhelms the mouth of the wicked, which opens a pair of sayings about how people will be remembered. The memory of the righteous will be a blessing, he says, but the name of the wicked will rot, like fruit that is left forgotten in a store. A village had a long memory in the ancient world, and the proverb reminds the young that the one thing they will certainly leave behind is a name.

The wise in heart accept commands, the writer says, but a chattering fool comes to ruin, and he places the listening mind beside the talking mouth. Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, and whoever takes crooked paths will be found out, for the honest traveller has nothing to hide and nothing to fear on the road. The saying treats honesty not as a burden but as a form of safety, so that the person who tells the truth need never remember what he said.

Hatred stirs up conflict, the writer says, but love covers over all wrongs, which is one of the most quoted sayings in the whole book. It does not mean that wrongs are hidden or denied, and most readers understand it as saying that love is willing to forgive and so to keep the peace. The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, he adds, but violence overwhelms the mouth of the wicked, which sets the water of a well beside the rumble of a storm.

The wealth of the rich is their fortified city, the writer observes, but poverty is the ruin of the poor, and he states the harsh fact without a word of excuse. He adds that whoever heeds discipline shows the way to life, and whoever ignores correction leads others astray, so that the wise person is also a guide and the foolish one a danger to his friends. Behind the two sayings stands the same idea, which is that every person is a signpost for somebody who walks behind.

Sin is not ended by multiplying words, the writer says, but the prudent hold their tongues, and the lesson will return many times in the book. The tongue of the righteous is choice silver, he adds, while the heart of the wicked is of little value, and the lips of the righteous nourish many, though fools die for lack of sense. A person's speech, in other words, is either a feast for others or a waste of breath, and the difference lies in whether he has first thought.

The blessing of the Lord brings wealth, the writer says, and he adds no trouble to it, which reminds the reader that riches taken from the wrong hands are often paid for in sorrow. What the wicked dread will overtake them, but what the righteous desire will be granted, he says, and when the storm has swept by, the wicked are gone, while the righteous stand firm forever. The image is of a village after a gale, in which the houses that were built on rock are still standing in the morning light.

The fear of the Lord adds length to life, the writer says, though the years of the wicked are cut short, and he does not claim that the rule has no exceptions but offers it as a hope. The prospect of the righteous is joy, but the hopes of the wicked come to nothing, and the way of the Lord is a refuge for the blameless, though it is destruction to evildoers. The righteous will never be uprooted, he says, while the wicked will not remain in the land, and the mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but a perverse tongue will be silenced.

The eleventh chapter opens with a saying about the marketplace, which says that dishonest scales are an abomination to the Lord, but that accurate weights are his delight. In an age when grain and silver were measured out by hand, a merchant with a false weight could cheat a whole village without raising his voice. The proverb takes what looks like a small matter of business and makes it a matter of faith, as if every honest sale were a quiet act of worship.

When pride comes, the writer says, then comes disgrace, but with humility comes wisdom, and the two halves of the saying belong together like the two sides of a coin. The integrity of the upright guides them, he adds, but the unfaithful are destroyed by their own duplicity, so that a crooked person is brought down by the very twists that he made. The thought is that honesty gives a person a map to follow, while deceit leaves him lost in a maze of his own making.

Wealth is worthless in the day of wrath, the writer says, but righteousness delivers from death, which is a sober reminder that some crises are beyond the power of money. The righteousness of the blameless makes their paths straight, he adds, but the wicked are brought down by their own wickedness, and the righteousness of the upright rescues them while the unfaithful are trapped by their own desires. A man might arrive at the river with a full purse and find that his money cannot carry him across.

When the righteous prosper, the city rejoices, the writer says, and when the wicked perish, there are shouts of joy, and the reader sees that goodness is not a private matter but a gift to the whole town. Through the blessing of the upright a city is exalted, but by the mouth of the wicked it is destroyed, which shows how the words of a few people can raise or ruin a community. The proverb is the voice of a village that remembers who made the common life better and who made it worse.

Whoever derides his neighbour has no sense, the writer says, but the person of understanding holds his tongue, and he advises restraint in a world where gossip is cheap. A gossip betrays a confidence, he adds, but a trustworthy person keeps a secret, so that one person's words leak like water from a cracked jar and the other is a safe place for another's trouble. In a small village, where everyone knew everyone, this was probably the most valuable of all reputations.

For lack of guidance a nation falls, the writer says, but victory is won through many advisers, and the saying reminds the powerful that no ruler sees everything alone. He follows it with a warning about the dangers of putting up security for a stranger, for whoever does so will surely suffer, but whoever refuses to shake hands on such things is safe. Both sayings are about the same thing in different dress, which is the value of a cautious second opinion before a person commits himself.

A kindhearted woman gains honour, the writer says, but ruthless men gain only wealth, which sets two kinds of success side by side and shows which is worth more. Those who are kind benefit themselves, he adds, but the cruel bring ruin on themselves, for kindness returns to the giver like a coin that is thrown into a well and comes back as water. It is one of many places in the book where the writer insists that the moral life and the happy life are not two roads but one.

One person gives freely, the writer says, and yet gains even more, while another withholds what he should give and comes to poverty, which is a paradox that has puzzled readers for centuries. A generous person will prosper, he adds, and whoever refreshes others will be refreshed, though people will curse the one who hoards grain and ask God's blessing on the one who is willing to sell. Most readers understand the saying not as a promise of profit but as a description of a community in which generosity builds trust, and trust in the end builds wealth.

Whoever seeks good finds favour, the writer says, but evil comes to the one who searches for it, and he adds that a person usually finds what he spends his days looking for. Those who trust in their riches will fall, but the righteous will thrive like a green leaf, and a person who brings ruin on his own household inherits only the wind. The fool, he concludes, will be a servant to the wise, which suggests that those who refuse to learn will one day work for those who did.

Like a gold ring in a pig's snout, the writer says, is a beautiful woman who shows no discretion, and the picture is deliberately comic, since a fine ornament has been placed where it cannot be admired. The saying means that beauty without good sense is wasted, in the same way that a jewel is wasted on an animal that rolls in the mud. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, the writer adds, and whoever wins people over is wise, which is a gentler picture to end the chapter on.

Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, the writer says, but whoever hates correction is stupid, and the twelfth chapter begins with words that are blunt on purpose. A good person obtains favour from the Lord, he adds, but the Lord condemns those who devise wicked schemes, and no one is established by wickedness, while the righteous cannot be uprooted. The root is the picture that the passage keeps, since a plant that is shallow may look green for a season but is gone with the first wind.

A wife of noble character is her husband's crown, the writer says, but she who brings shame is like decay in his bones, and the saying speaks of a household in which marriage is a partnership. Better to be a nobody and have a servant, he adds, than to pretend to be somebody and have no food, which mocks those who put on a show of wealth they do not have. The two sayings are about the same thing, which is that what matters in a home is the substance of its life and not its outward display.

The righteous care for the needs of their animals, the writer says, but the kindest acts of the wicked are cruel, which is a surprising and gentle saying to find in a book of wisdom. The animals were the wealth of a farm, and a person's treatment of the ox that pulled his plough was thought to show his whole character. Those who work their land will have abundant food, he adds, but those who chase fantasies have no sense, since the soil gives nothing to the dreamer who will not dig.

The way of fools seems right to them, the writer says, but the wise listen to advice, and the saying reaches the centre of the book's view of folly, which is that the fool is certain. A fool shows his annoyance at once, he adds, but the prudent overlook an insult, since there is strength in being able to let a hot word pass and cool down. A person who must answer every slight is a prisoner of the last person who spoke to him, and the proverb offers freedom to anyone who will learn to wait.

An honest witness tells the truth, the writer says, but a false witness tells lies, and then he gives the chapter its most memorable line, saying that the words of the reckless pierce like swords. The tongue of the wise brings healing, he adds, and truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment, because a lie must be fed by further lies, and sooner or later it is found out. The saying gives the same organ two uses, as a blade that cuts and as a hand that binds up the wound.

There is deceit in the hearts of those who plot evil, the writer says, but joy for those who promote peace, and no harm overtakes the righteous, while the wicked have their fill of trouble. The Lord detests lying lips, he adds, but delights in people who are trustworthy, and then comes a quiet saying about worry, which says that anxiety weighs down the heart, but a kind word cheers it up. It is one of the shortest proverbs in the book, and many readers find it the most true to life.

Diligent hands will rule, the writer says, but the slothful will be put to forced labour, and he shows that ability and character, in the end, decide who commands and who serves. The righteous choose their friends carefully, he adds, but the way of the wicked leads them astray, and the lazy do not roast any game, while the diligent feed on the riches of the hunt. In the way of righteousness there is life, he concludes, and along that path there is no death, a line that closes the chapter on a note of unusual hope.

A wise child heeds a father's instruction, the writer says at the start of the thirteenth chapter, but a mocker does not respond to rebuke, and one can almost hear the parent behind the saying. From the fruit of their lips people enjoy good things, he adds, but the unfaithful have an appetite for violence, and whoever guards his lips preserves his life, while he who speaks rashly will come to ruin. The proverb thus makes a person's mouth a gate which can be left open in carelessness or watched with care.

A sluggard craves and gets nothing, the writer says, but the desires of the diligent are fully satisfied, and one person pretends to be rich yet has nothing, while another pretends to be poor yet has great wealth. Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little makes it grow, which is the oldest advice in the world about saving. The picture is of a farmer who adds one coin at a time to a clay jar, and who is rich in the end because he did not hurry.

Hope deferred makes the heart sick, the writer says, but a longing fulfilled is a tree of life, and few sentences in the book are so quickly understood by someone who has waited for a letter or a friend. Walk with the wise and become wise, he adds, for a companion of fools suffers harm, and a good person leaves an inheritance for his children's children, whereas the wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous. The chapter thus ends on the idea of company, which means that a person is shaped by those he walks beside.

The wise woman builds her house, the writer says at the start of the fourteenth chapter, but with her own hands the foolish one tears hers down, and the saying sets two builders side by side. Whoever walks uprightly fears the Lord, he adds, but whoever is devious in his ways despises him, and a fool's talk brings a rod to his back, while the lips of the wise protect them. A home, in this view, is not simply a place but something that people make or unmake every day by the way they speak and live.

Where there are no oxen, the writer says, the manger is empty, but from the strength of an ox come abundant harvests, and the saying is a rare piece of farm humour in a serious book. A clean stable is a comfortable sight, but it means that no work is being done, and so the one who wants a full barn must be willing to put up with a certain amount of mess. He adds a word about company, advising his reader to stay away from a fool, since there is no knowledge to be found on his lips.

There is a way that seems right to a person, the writer says, but in the end it leads to death, and the same saying returns in the sixteenth chapter, as if it were too important to say once. Even in laughter the heart may ache, he adds, and joy may end in grief, and he sees that appearances can deceive both a traveller and the person who watches him. The simple believe anything, he says, but the prudent give thought to their steps, so the remedy for an attractive road is to stop and look before walking.

A quick-tempered person does foolish things, the writer says, and a crafty person is hated, but whoever is patient has great understanding, whereas the one who is quick-tempered displays folly. A heart at peace gives life to the body, he adds, but envy rots the bones, which is an old way of saying that the state of the mind is written on the whole person. The sayings suggest that self-control is both a moral virtue and a practical wisdom, since the calm person sees more than the person who is carried away.

The poor are shunned even by their neighbours, the writer says, but the rich have many friends, and he observes the world as it is before he says how it ought to be. Whoever despises a neighbour sins, but blessed is the one who is kind to the needy, he adds, and whoever oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honours God. The idea that the poor person is made by the same hand as the rich is one of the great themes of the book.

All hard work brings a profit, the writer says, but mere talk leads only to poverty, and it is easy to imagine him smiling at the market place where so much was said and so little done. The crown of the wise is their wealth, he adds, but the folly of fools yields folly, and a truthful witness saves lives, while a false witness is deceitful. The sayings turn on the difference between talk and work and between honest and false words, which are the chief concerns of the whole chapter.

Righteousness exalts a nation, the writer says, but sin condemns any people, and the proverb takes the same idea that has shaped his advice to a single person and applies it to a whole country. A king delights in a wise servant, he adds, but his anger falls on one who acts shamefully, so that even in the court a person's character counts for more than his title. To an ancient reader, living in a small kingdom beside great empires, such a thought would have carried a good deal of weight.

A gentle answer turns away wrath, the writer says at the opening of the fifteenth chapter, but a harsh word stirs up anger, and there are few sentences in the book that have been so widely repeated. The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge, he adds, but the mouth of fools gushes folly, and the contrast is between speech that makes a truth beautiful and speech that pours out everything it contains. The gentle answer is not weakness but a form of strength, since it takes more mastery to speak softly in anger than to shout.

The eyes of the Lord are everywhere, the writer says, keeping watch on the wicked and the good, and a happy heart makes the face cheerful, but heartache crushes the spirit. All the days of the oppressed are wretched, he adds, but the cheerful heart has a continual feast, and better a small portion of vegetables where there is love than a fattened calf with hatred. The meal in the proverb is simple, but the people sitting at it are at peace, and that is what gives it its flavour.

Plans fail for lack of counsel, the writer says, but with many advisers they succeed, and a person finds joy in giving an apt reply, for how good is a timely word. Whoever heeds life-giving correction will be at home among the wise, he adds, and the fear of the Lord teaches a person wisdom, and humility comes before honour. The chapter ends on the idea that learning is a lifelong task, so that the person who is willing to be taught will never be shut out from the company of the wise.

To humans belong the plans of the heart, the writer says at the start of the sixteenth chapter, but from the Lord comes the reply of the tongue. All a person's ways seem pure to him, but the Lord weighs the motives, he adds, so commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans. In the heart a person plans his course, but the Lord establishes his steps, which means that a wise person plans carefully and then holds his plans with an open hand.

Pride goes before destruction, the writer says, and a haughty spirit before a fall, and it is among the most quoted lines in the entire book. Better to be lowly in spirit and among the poor, he adds, than to share plunder with the proud, since a humble person who has little can sleep at night, while the proud person who has much cannot. The picture is of a tower built too high and too fast, which looks splendid in the morning and by evening has begun to lean.

A king delights in honest lips, the writer says, and he loves anyone who speaks what is right, and the proverb shows what a ruler most needs and rarely gets. A king's wrath is a messenger of death, he adds, but a wise person will appease it, and when a king's face brightens, it means life, and his favour is like a rain cloud in the spring. To a farmer in a dry country, no comparison could be more generous, since the rain of spring decided whether the year would be one of plenty.

How much better to get wisdom than gold, the writer says, and to choose understanding rather than silver, and he returns to a comparison that the book loves. Whoever gives heed to instruction prospers, he adds, and blessed is the person who trusts in the Lord, and the wise in heart are called discerning, so that pleasant words promote instruction. Gracious words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones, and the saying hints that kindness has an effect on the body as well as the mind.

A scoundrel plots evil, the writer says, and on his lips it is like a scorching fire, which is a bold image of the harm that a few cruel words can do. A perverse person stirs up conflict, he adds, and a gossip separates close friends, and a violent person entices his neighbour and leads him down a path that is not good. Such a man never works alone, and the saying warns that the greatest harm of a troublemaker is the harm that he persuades other people to do.

Grey hair is a crown of splendour, the writer says, and it is attained in the way of righteousness, so that old age is honoured when it is the fruit of a good life. Better a patient person than a warrior, he adds, and one with self-control than one who takes a city, and the saying places the quiet victory over temper above the loud victory of the battlefield. The lot is cast into the lap, he concludes, but its every decision is from the Lord, a reminder that, even in chance, ancient Israel looked for a purpose.

Better a dry crust with peace and quiet, the writer says at the start of the seventeenth chapter, than a house full of feasting, with strife, and few sayings tell so well of a happy home. Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, he adds, and parents are the pride of their children, so the generations are pictured as honouring one another across the years. The table in the proverb is plain, but the people sitting around it are at peace, and for the writer that is worth more than any amount of meat.

The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, the writer says, but the Lord tests the heart, and the image is of a refiner who melts away the dross. Starting a quarrel is like breaking a dam, he adds, so drop the matter before a dispute breaks out, and whoever covers an offence promotes love, but whoever repeats the matter separates close friends. A little crack in a dam seems harmless, but once the water begins to flow nobody can say where it will stop.

A friend loves at all times, the writer says, and a brother is born for a time of adversity, which is one of the best-loved proverbs in the book. A cheerful heart is good medicine, he adds, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones, and a person who is glad is helped by it in body as well as in mind. The two sayings together describe the best support that anyone can have, which is a friend who stays when things are bad and a spirit that has not given up.

A discerning person keeps wisdom in view, the writer says, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth, like a mind that looks everywhere except at what is in front of it. The one who has knowledge uses words with restraint, he adds, and the one who has understanding is even-tempered, and even a fool who keeps silent is thought wise, and he who holds his tongue is thought discerning. It is a gentle joke, and a useful one, which says that silence is often the best disguise a fool can wear.

The eighteenth chapter opens with a person who separates himself from others, who seeks his own desires and quarrels against all sound judgment, and the writer implies that wisdom needs company. A fool finds no pleasure in understanding, he adds, but delights in airing his own opinions, and the words of a person's mouth are deep waters, while the fountain of wisdom is a rushing stream. Between the fool and the wise lies the difference between a puddle that is stirred by every foot and a spring that never runs dry.

The name of the Lord is a fortified tower, the writer says, and the righteous run to it and are safe, like villagers who see raiders on the hill and hurry for the shelter of the walls. The wealth of the rich is their fortified city, he adds, and in their imagination it is a lofty wall, so that the proverb suggests that the safety bought with money is more a feeling than a fact. A tower that is real can be run to, but a wall that exists only in the mind will not shelter anyone when the storm comes.

Before a downfall the heart is proud, the writer says, but humility comes before honour, and the pair of sayings repeats a pattern that the book loves. To answer before listening, he adds, is folly and shame, and it is easy to picture the impatient young man who has his reply ready before the old man has finished his sentence. The saying is short and sharp, and a reader who has ever cut across another person's words will probably wince as he reads it.

The human spirit can endure sickness, the writer says, but who can bear a crushed spirit, and so he places the courage of the mind above the strength of the body. The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, he adds, and the ears of the wise seek it out, and the first to put his case seems right, until someone else comes forward and cross-examines him. Courts of the ancient world met at the city gate, and those who sat there would have known well how a story sounds different when the second speaker has had his say.

The casting of the lot settles disputes, the writer says, and keeps strong opponents apart, a statement of how an ancient community kept the peace when argument failed. An offended brother is harder to win back than a fortified city, he adds, and quarrels are like the bars of a castle, so the walls between hurt people are the hardest to break. The saying comes from a keen observer of family life, who knows that the longest silences are often found between the closest people.

From the fruit of their mouths people have their fill, the writer says, and with the harvest of their lips they are satisfied, and then he gives one of the most quoted lines in the book. The tongue has the power of life and death, he says, and those who love it will eat its fruit, so a person must live with whatever his words have grown. He who finds a wife finds what is good and receives favour from the Lord, the writer adds, which turns from speech to home life without pausing to draw breath.

A poor person pleads for mercy, the writer says, but a rich person answers harshly, which is another of the plain pictures of an unequal world. One who has unreliable friends soon comes to ruin, he adds, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother, and real friendship is not measured by how many people one knows. A person may have a crowd around him and still be alone, while another may have only one friend and be rich in the things that count.

Better a poor person whose walk is blameless, the writer says at the start of the nineteenth chapter, than a fool whose lips are perverse, for honesty is worth more than the show of success. Desire without knowledge is not good, he adds, and whoever is hasty with his feet misses his way, and a person's own folly ruins his life, yet his heart rages against the Lord. It is a perceptive saying about blame, which observes that people who have made a mess of things are often the quickest to complain about the world.

Wealth adds many friends, the writer says, but a poor person is deserted even by his neighbour, and he states the sad truth that friendship is sometimes bought. A false witness will not go unpunished, he adds, and whoever pours out lies will not go free, and many curry favour with a ruler, and everyone is the friend of a person who gives gifts. The poor person's relatives all shun him, and even his friends keep far from him, which makes the proverb a description of how the world is, not an approval of it.

A person's wisdom yields patience, the writer says, and it is to one's glory to overlook an offence, a line that has comforted many people who found it hard to forgive. Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, he adds, and he will reward them for what they have done, which puts the poor man's need on the same footing as God's own debt. Many are the plans in a person's heart, but it is the Lord's purpose that prevails, and so the chapter ends with a reminder that human schemes must be carried out under a larger design.

The lazy person buries his hand in the dish, the writer says, and is too tired to bring it back to his mouth, which is one of the funniest pictures in the whole book. In the twentieth chapter he adds that wine is a mocker and beer a brawler, and whoever is led astray by them is not wise, while the one who will not plough in autumn will find no harvest. The proverbs make a small comedy of excuses and show how idleness and drink can each cost a person his living.

The purposes of the human heart are deep waters, the writer says, but one who has insight draws them out, which compares a mind to a well from which only a patient person can raise a bucket. A king's wrath is like the roar of a lion, he adds, and to avoid strife is honourable for a person, though every fool is quick to quarrel. Together the sayings suggest that the wise listen to what lies below the surface, and that they keep out of a fight that would only prove their foolishness.

Many a person claims to have unfailing love, the writer says, but who can find someone who is truly trustworthy, and it is a sad, dry observation about how easily the word love is spent. The righteous walk in their integrity, he adds, and blessed are their children after them, which makes a father's character the first inheritance he leaves to his family. Who can say, he asks, that he has kept his heart pure and is clean from sin, and the question is meant to make the reader humble.

It is no good, it is no good, says the buyer, but then off he goes and boasts about what he has bought, and the writer sketches a scene that anyone who has been to a market will know. Food gained by fraud tastes sweet, he adds, but one day the mouth will be full of gravel, which means that cheating pays at first and costs more at the end. Honest weights and measures are a theme to which the book returns, and the Lord, it says, detests the use of two kinds of weight.

There is gold, and there are rubies in abundance, the writer says, but lips that speak knowledge are a rare jewel, and so the person who speaks wisely is worth more than the whole of a jeweller's stock. Do not say, I will pay you back for this wrong, he warns, but wait for the Lord, and he will avenge you, which turns the wish for revenge into patience and trust. A person's steps are directed by the Lord, he adds, and how then can anyone understand their own way, a question that has no easy answer.

The human spirit is the lamp of the Lord, the writer says, and it searches out the inmost being, so that each person carries a small light that shows him his own heart. Love and faithfulness keep a king safe, he adds, and through love his throne is made secure, and the glory of young men is their strength, while the splendour of the old is their grey hair. Each age of life has a gift of its own, and the saying asks each generation to honour the other.

The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, the writer says at the start of the twenty-first chapter, like a stream of water, and he channels it wherever he pleases. A farmer in a dry land would know at once what he meant, because to turn a stream into the right ditch with a few strokes of a spade is to bring a field to life. All a person's ways seem right to him, he adds, but the Lord weighs the heart, and to do what is right and just is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice.

Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the writer says, are sin, and the plans of the diligent lead to profit as surely as haste leads to poverty, while a fortune made by lying is a fleeting vapour. Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, he adds, will also cry out and not be answered, and the wise store up choice food and olive oil, but a foolish person gulps his down. The saying about the poor is the heart of the chapter, since it says that the way we treat the weak will be the way we are treated.

Better to live on a corner of the roof, the writer says, than to share a house with a quarrelling person, and a flat roof in Israel was a place where one could sit alone. Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue, he adds, keeps himself from calamity, and no wisdom, no insight, no plan can succeed against the Lord. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, he concludes, but victory rests with the Lord, which was a bold thing to say in a world that trusted its chariots and cavalry.

A good name is more desirable than great riches, the writer says at the start of the twenty-second chapter, and to be esteemed is better than silver or gold. Rich and poor have this in common, he adds, that the Lord is the maker of them all, and then comes one of the most famous sayings of the book. It says to start a child on the way he should go, and even when old he will not turn from it, which most readers take as a general rule and not a promise.

At the twenty-second chapter a new section begins, called the Sayings of the Wise, in which the writer speaks directly to his student, saying, pay attention and listen, and apply your heart to what I teach. It will be pleasing, he says, if you keep these sayings in your heart, so that your trust may be in the Lord, and he speaks of thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge. Many scholars notice that this part of the book closely resembles an Egyptian teaching known as the Instruction of Amenemope, which suggests that wise men of different lands shared and borrowed from one another.

Do not exploit the poor because they are poor, the writer says, and do not crush the needy in court, for the Lord will take up their case and will plunder those who plunder them. Do not make friends with a hot-tempered person, he adds, and do not associate with one easily angered, or you may learn his ways and get yourself ensnared. A bad temper, like a cold, passes easily from one person to another, and the wise do not sit too long in the company of those who have it.

Do not be one of those who shake hands in pledge or put up security for debts, the writer warns, for if you lack the means to pay, your very bed will be snatched from under you. Do you see someone skilled in their work, he asks, and the answer is that they will serve before kings and will not serve before officials of low rank. The two sayings lie close together, and between them they describe the two ways to a secure life, which are to avoid rash promises and to become very good at something.

When you sit to dine with a ruler, the writer says, note well what is before you, and put a knife to your throat if you are greedy, a vivid way of telling a guest to keep firm control. Do not crave his delicacies, he adds, for that food may be deceptive, and do not eat the food of a begrudging host, for he is the kind of person who is always calculating the cost. The fine dishes of the powerful may be the bait in a trap, and the wise young person eats little and watches closely.

Do not wear yourself out to get rich, the writer says, for when your eyes light on wealth, it is gone, and it makes wings for itself and flies off to the sky like an eagle. The saying does not condemn work or honest profit but the restless chase after more, which can eat up the strength and time that a person needs for better things. He adds that you should not speak to a fool, who will only despise the good sense of your words.

Do not move an ancient boundary stone, the writer says, nor encroach on the fields of the fatherless, for their Defender is strong, and he will take up their case against you. Boundary stones marked the edge of a family's land, and to move one by night was a quiet theft that a widow or an orphan could hardly resist. Apply your heart to instruction, he adds, and do not withhold discipline from a child, a saying that readers apply in different ways, though most agree that it asks parents to guide and not to ignore.

My son, if your heart is wise, the father says, then my heart will rejoice, and my inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right. Listen to your father, who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old, he adds, and buy the truth and do not sell it, along with wisdom, instruction and insight. The father of a righteous child has great joy, he concludes, and may your father and mother be glad, and may she who gave you birth rejoice.

Do not let your heart envy sinners, the writer says, but always continue in the fear of the Lord, for there is surely a future hope for you, and your hope will not be cut off. In the next chapter he adds that you should not envy the wicked or desire their company, for their hearts plot violence and their lips talk about making trouble. By wisdom a house is built, he says, and through understanding it is established, and through knowledge its rooms are filled with rare and beautiful treasures.

Do not join those who drink too much wine or gorge themselves on meat, the writer says, for drunkards and gluttons become poor, and drowsiness clothes them in rags. Then he asks a series of questions, wondering who has woe and who has sorrow, who has strife and who has complaints, and he answers that it is those who linger over wine. In the end it bites like a snake and poisons like a viper, he says, and the drinker will see strange sights and feel like one lying at the top of a mast, a plain picture of the cost.

The righteous fall seven times and rise again, the writer says near the end of the twenty-fourth chapter, but the wicked stumble when calamity strikes, so the difference is not that one never falls but that one gets up. Do not gloat when your enemy falls, he adds, and do not let your heart rejoice when he stumbles, or the Lord will see it and be displeased. Then he tells of passing the field of a lazy man, which was overgrown with thorns and whose wall was in ruins, and says, I saw and learned a lesson.

The twenty-fifth chapter begins with a note that these also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, copied out, and so we learn a little of how the collection came to be. It is the glory of God to conceal a matter, the writer says, and the glory of kings to search it out, which gives a ruler the task of a scholar who does not rest until a problem is understood. It is a rare idea in the ancient world, that the powerful should be curious and that hidden things are an invitation and not a threat.

As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, the writer says, so the hearts of kings are unsearchable, and the saying is both respectful and a little wary of the power of a king's mind. Remove the dross from the silver, he continues, and a silversmith can fashion a vessel, and remove the wicked from the king's presence, and his throne will be established through righteousness. The saying is a lesson in government, which says that a ruler is no better than the company he keeps.

Do not exalt yourself in the king's presence, the writer says, and do not claim a place among his great men, for it is better to be told, come up here, than to be humbled in front of a noble. The advice is both worldly and wise, since the one who takes a lower place may be moved up while the one who takes a higher place may be sent down in front of all. He adds a word about quarrels, saying not to rush into court but to argue the case with your neighbour first, and not to betray another man's confidence.

A word aptly spoken, the writer says, is like apples of gold in settings of silver, and the picture is of a fruit carved in gold in a bowl of silver, a thing both costly and beautiful. Like an earring of gold is the rebuke of a wise person to a listening ear, he adds, and the point is that the same words are a treasure to the person who is ready to hear them. The two sayings suggest that good speech depends not only on the speaker but also on the moment and the listener.

Like the coolness of snow at harvest time is a trustworthy messenger to those who send him, the writer says, for he refreshes his master's spirit, as anyone who has worked in a harvest field will know. Like clouds and wind without rain, he adds, is one who boasts of gifts he does not give, since all that he offers is the promise of a storm. Through patience a ruler can be persuaded, he concludes, and a gentle tongue can break a bone, which is a paradox about the surprising strength of soft words.

If you find honey, the writer says, eat just enough, for too much of it will make you vomit, and the saying is a plain warning that even good things can be too much of a good thing. Seldom set foot in your neighbour's house, he adds, or he will have too much of you and will hate you, and he is a shrewd observer of friendship, which needs distance as well as nearness. Honey was among the great pleasures of the ancient world, and the proverb treats it as a test of self-control.

Whoever gives false testimony against a neighbour, the writer says, is like a club or a sword or a sharp arrow, since a false word wounds as surely as a weapon. Confidence in a faithless person in a time of trouble, he adds, is like a broken tooth or a lame foot, and singing songs to a heavy heart is like taking away a garment on a cold day. The last of these shows the writer's gentle understanding, because he knows that it is possible to be cheerful at the wrong time and so do harm.

If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, the writer says, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, and it is one of the most famous commands of the book. In doing this, he adds, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the Lord will reward you, and the burning coals are often read as a way of shaming a person into goodness, though not all readers agree. The Apostle Paul quotes the saying in his letter to the Romans, which shows how long the thought has been valued in the Jewish and Christian traditions.

The north wind brings rain, the writer says, and a sly tongue brings angry looks, which uses the weather as a way of saying that certain causes bring certain results. Like a muddied spring or a polluted well is a righteous person who gives way to the wicked, he adds, for a well that was once clear and a source of life now sickens those who drink from it. The saying is about the fall of a good person who has compromised, and the harm that this does to everyone who looked to him for goodness.

Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land, the writer says, and anyone who has waited for a letter from someone far away will know what he means. Like a city whose walls are broken through is a person who lacks self-control, he adds, and the picture is of a town that is open to every attacker and that has no defence against the next mistake. The twenty-fifth chapter ends there, on a note of self-mastery, as a reminder that the best defence a person has is a disciplined heart.

Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, the writer says at the start of the twenty-sixth chapter, honour is not fitting for a fool, like weather that is out of its season. Like a fluttering sparrow or a darting swallow, he adds, an undeserved curse does not come to rest, which comforts the reader with the thought that a groundless insult will fly away like a bird. A whip is for the horse, a halter for the donkey, and a rod for the backs of fools, he concludes, and the book is blunt about those who will not be taught.

Do not answer a fool according to his folly, one verse says, or you will be like him, and the next verse says to answer a fool according to his folly, or he will think himself wise. The two sayings seem to contradict one another, and the book has put them side by side as if to say that no rule can replace judgment, since a fool must sometimes be answered and sometimes left alone. Jewish and Christian readers have long taken this as a lesson that wisdom is a skill for knowing which saying fits which moment.

Sending a message by the hand of a fool, the writer says, is like cutting off one's own feet and inviting violence, and the point is that an important errand needs a reliable person. Like a lame man's legs that hang limp is a proverb in the mouth of a fool, he adds, and like tying a stone in a sling is the giving of honour to a fool. A stone that is tied into a sling can never be thrown, which makes the honour as useless as the gift of a good saying to a person who will not use it.

As a dog goes back to what it has left on the ground, the writer says, so a fool repeats his folly, and it shows how some people keep going back to what harmed them. Do you see a person wise in his own eyes, he then asks, and he answers that there is more hope for a fool than for him. The idea is that a person who knows he is foolish can still learn, while one who is satisfied with his own wisdom has shut the door on learning.

The sluggard says, there is a lion in the road, a fierce lion roaming the streets, and the excuse is so grand that it becomes comic. As a door turns on its hinges, the writer says, so a sluggard turns on his bed, and he buries his hand in the dish and is too weary to bring it back to his mouth. In his own eyes the sluggard is wiser than seven people who answer discreetly, which suggests that the laziest people are often the ones who are most pleased with themselves.

Without wood a fire goes out, the writer says, and without a gossip a quarrel dies down, and there is a simple, practical wisdom in that. As charcoal to embers and as wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome person for kindling strife, he adds, and the words of a gossip are like choice morsels, which go down to the inmost parts. People pass on a bit of gossip with the pleasure of a snack, the saying hints, but the harm it does goes deeper than the pleasure.

Like a coating of silver glaze over earthenware are fervent lips with a wicked heart, the writer says, a picture of a plain clay pot that has been painted to shine like precious metal.
