Whoever hates disguises it with his lips, he adds, but inside he harbours deceit, and when his speech is charming, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart. Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, he concludes, and a stone will roll back on the one who starts it rolling, so that a cunning plan can turn on the planner.

Do not boast about tomorrow, the writer says at the start of the twenty-seventh chapter, for you do not know what a day may bring, which reminds the reader that the future is a country that no one has seen. Let someone else praise you, and not your own mouth, he adds, a stranger and not your own lips, and a stone is heavy and sand is a burden, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both. Anger is cruel and fury overwhelming, he says, but who can stand before jealousy, and the sayings show that the feelings of the heart can be heavier than rocks.

Better is open rebuke than hidden love, the writer says, and wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses, for the truth that hurts is kinder than the flattery that harms. Perfume and incense bring joy to the heart, he adds, and the pleasantness of a friend springs from sincere advice, and a neighbour nearby is better than a relative far away. Anyone who has been grateful for an honest word from a friend will know what the writer means, and the saying has comforted many who have had to hear hard things from people who loved them.

As iron sharpens iron, the writer says, so one person sharpens another, and the line has become one of the most quoted in the book because it is true of friendship, of teaching and of work. As water reflects the face, so a person's heart reflects the person, he adds, and then he turns to the farmer, saying that one should know well the condition of one's flocks and give careful attention to the herds. For riches do not endure forever, he explains, and neither does a crown last for all generations, but the care of a good farmer feeds the household and makes a living.

The wicked flee when no one pursues, the writer says at the start of the twenty-eighth chapter, but the righteous are as bold as a lion, a sharp picture of how a guilty conscience sees enemies everywhere. When a country is in revolt it has many rulers, he adds, but a ruler with discernment and knowledge maintains order, which means that a nation does better with one wise leader than with many quarrelling ones. Honesty is the root of the saying, since a person with nothing to hide has nothing to run from.

A ruler who oppresses the poor, the writer says, is like a driving rain that leaves no crops, and it is a bitter irony that the one whose task is to protect the people becomes the storm that destroys them. Those who forsake instruction praise the wicked, he adds, but those who keep instruction resist them, and better a poor person whose walk is blameless than one whose ways are crooked, though he is rich. Even the prayers of a person who turns a deaf ear to the law are detestable, the passage warns, which links worship with the way a person treats others.

Whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit, the writer says, and the rich are wise in their own eyes, but the poor who have discernment see through them. When the righteous triumph there is great elation, he adds, but when the wicked rise, people go into hiding, and then he gives a verse that readers have loved for its kindness. Whoever conceals his sins does not prosper, but the one who confesses and renounces them finds mercy.

Blessed is the one who always trembles before God, the writer says, but he who hardens his heart falls into trouble, and then he turns to those who hold power. Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a helpless people, he adds, for a tyrant has no judgment, but one who hates ill-gotten gain will enjoy a long reign. The saying ties the length of a reign to a ruler's honesty, which was a bold thing to say in a time when kings were thought to rule by right.

Those who work their land will have abundant food, the writer says, but those who chase fantasies will have their fill of poverty, and he returns to the lesson of the farmer and the dreamer. A faithful person will be richly blessed, he adds, but one eager to get rich will not go unpunished, and a person who is stingy is eager for wealth and does not realise that poverty is waiting for him. The lines remind the reader that haste to be rich is a different thing from the steady work that leads to plenty.

Whoever rebukes a person will in the end gain more favour than one who has a flattering tongue, the writer says, which is another of the book's praises of honest speech. Whoever gives to the poor will lack nothing, he adds, but whoever closes his eyes to them receives many curses, and so the passage ends with one of the plainest teachings about charity in the entire book. A greedy person stirs up conflict, he says, but the one who trusts in the Lord will prosper, and those who trust in themselves are fools, but those who walk in wisdom are kept safe.

A person who stiffens his neck after many rebukes, the writer says at the start of the twenty-ninth chapter, will suddenly be destroyed without remedy, and it is a grim saying about those who will never listen. When the righteous thrive, the people rejoice, he adds, but when the wicked rule, the people groan, and a person who loves wisdom brings joy to his father, though one who wastes his wealth does the opposite. By justice a king gives a country stability, he concludes, but those who are greedy for bribes tear it down, so that a town's happiness rests on the honesty of those who rule it.

Those who flatter their neighbours, the writer says, are spreading a net for their feet, and evildoers are snared by their own sin, but the righteous can sing and be glad. The righteous care about justice for the poor, he adds, but the wicked have no such concern, and mockers stir up a city, but the wise turn away anger. A fool gives full vent to his anger, he concludes, but a wise person keeps himself under control, which is a short lesson on the way in which a few calm people can keep a whole town at peace.

If a ruler listens to lies, the writer says, all his officials become wicked, because the people around a ruler soon learn what he wishes to hear. The poor and the oppressor have this in common, he adds, that the Lord gives sight to the eyes of both, and if a king judges the poor with fairness, his throne will be established forever. A child left undisciplined disgraces his mother, he adds, and a person should discipline his child, who will then bring peace and give delight to his heart.

Where there is no revelation, the writer says, the people cast off restraint, but blessed is the one who heeds wisdom's instruction, and the word translated as revelation can also mean vision or guidance, so that translations differ. Do you see a person who speaks in haste, he asks, and the answer is that there is more hope for a fool than for him, while pride brings a person low and the lowly gain honour. The fear of man will prove to be a snare, he concludes, but whoever trusts in the Lord is kept safe, which is a fitting thought for the end of a long run of teaching on rulers and the ruled.

The thirtieth chapter begins with the words of Agur, son of Jakeh, whom the book gives no title and whose origins are unknown, and he opens with a confession of weariness. I am the most ignorant of men, he says, and I have not learned wisdom, and he asks who has gone up to heaven and come down, and who has gathered the wind in his hands. Who has wrapped up the waters in a cloak, he asks, and who has established the ends of the earth, and the questions stir a sense of wonder unlike the confident tone of the earlier chapters.

Every word of God is flawless, Agur says, and he is a shield to those who take refuge in him, which is a quiet statement of trust after the questions that have gone before. Do not add to his words, he warns, or he will rebuke you and prove you to be a liar, so a person should neither claim more than he knows nor speak for God without cause. The humility of the saying makes a fitting answer to the wonder of the chapter's first lines.

Two things I ask of you, Agur prays, and do not refuse me before I die, which are to keep falsehood and lies far from me, and to give me neither poverty nor riches. Give me only my daily bread, he asks, for otherwise I may have too much and disown you and say, who is the Lord, or I may become poor and steal and so dishonour the name of my God. It is among the most thoughtful prayers in the Hebrew Bible, since it asks for the middle path in which neither wealth nor want becomes a temptation.

Agur turns to the world he sees around him, and he describes a generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother, and warns in strong words against anyone who mocks their parents. There is a generation that is pure in its own eyes, he says, and yet is not washed of its filth, a generation whose eyes are so haughty, and whose eyelids are so lofty. There is a generation whose teeth are swords, he adds, and whose jaws are set with knives to devour the poor from the earth and the needy from among mankind.

The leech has two daughters, Agur says, and they cry, give, give, a quick picture of a greedy appetite that is never full. There are three things that are never satisfied, he says, and four that never say, enough, namely the grave, the longing of a childless woman, land that is never satisfied with water, and fire that never says, enough. The riddle is built to show that desire, like fire, grows with what it is fed, and that some hungers are not ended by anything the world can give.

There are three things that are too wonderful for me, Agur says, and four that I do not understand, and he sets the list out like a riddle. They are the way of an eagle in the sky, a snake on a rock, a ship on the high seas, and a man with a young woman, each of them a path that leaves no trace behind. The four wonders have in common that they are beautiful, quick and mysterious, and that a person can watch them for a lifetime without fully understanding them.

Under three things the earth trembles, Agur says, and under four it cannot bear up, among them a servant who becomes king, a fool who has plenty to eat and a maidservant who replaces her mistress. A few verses earlier he describes someone who does wrong, wipes her mouth and says that she has done nothing wrong, showing a person who is skilled at excusing herself. His point is that things go badly in a community when power or comfort fall into hands that have not been prepared for them.

Four things on earth are small, Agur says, yet they are extremely wise, and then he names them in order. Ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in summer, and hyraxes are creatures of little power, yet they make their home in the crags. Locusts have no king, he adds, yet they advance together in ranks, and a lizard can be caught in the hand, yet it is found in the palaces of kings, so even the smallest creatures can teach.

There are three things that are stately in their stride, Agur says, and four that move with stately bearing, which makes a second list in the poet's collection of numbers. The first is the lion, mightiest among the beasts, who retreats before nothing, and the next are a strutting rooster, a he-goat and a king secure against revolt. If you have played the fool by exalting yourself, or if you have planned evil, he adds, clap your hand over your mouth, which is a vivid way of telling the proud to hush.

For as churning cream produces butter, Agur concludes, and as twisting the nose produces blood, so stirring up anger produces strife, and he ends the chapter with a lesson drawn from the farmhouse. A woman working a churn in a bright kitchen knows that what she makes depends on how long and how hard she shakes the cream, and the same is true of a quarrel, which grows with every harsh word. The chapter closes without a final blessing, and the reader is left with the thought that wisdom is found in the humble work of the kitchen as much as in the great questions of the sky.

The thirty-first chapter opens with the words of King Lemuel, an inspired message that his mother taught him, and he is a king about whom nothing else is known. What, my son, she asks, what, son of my womb, what, son of my vows, and the repeated question has the urgency of a parent who has only one chance to say what matters. She tells him not to spend his strength on pleasures that ruin kings, so that her first advice is that a ruler must guard himself against the very things that destroy rulers.

It is not for kings, Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, nor for rulers to crave beer, her warning continues, lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and deprive all the oppressed of their rights. Let beer be for those who are perishing and wine for those in anguish, she adds, so that they may drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more. The advice is blunt and practical, since a king whose mind is clouded cannot judge, and the people who depend on his judgment will pay the price.

Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, the queen mother says, for the rights of all who are destitute, and speak up and judge fairly, and defend the rights of the poor and needy. In a few lines she turns from what a king should avoid to what he should do, so that the true use of power is shown to be the defence of the powerless. It is among the strongest calls for justice in the whole book, and it appears, of all places, in a mother's advice to her son.

The poem that closes the book is an acrostic, which means that in Hebrew each verse begins with the next letter of the alphabet in turn, as though the writer wished to praise this woman from first letter to last. A wife of noble character, who can find, it begins, and the question is not so much doubtful as admiring, for she is worth far more than rubies. The phrase recalls the opening chapters, where Wisdom was said to be more precious than rubies, and so the reader is already invited to see more than a simple portrait.

Her husband has full confidence in her, the poem says, and he lacks nothing of value, for she brings him good and not harm all the days of her life. There is no suggestion here of a woman who is merely kept at home, since her husband's confidence rests on her skill, her honesty and her good sense. The marriage is pictured as a partnership in which each side trusts the other with all that matters, and in which the trust has been earned over many years.

She selects wool and flax and works with eager hands, the poem says, and she is like the merchant ships, bringing her food from afar. She gets up while it is still night, and she provides food for her family and portions for her servant girls, so that her day begins long before anyone else's. The comparison to ships is bold, since it makes a woman at her loom as enterprising as a captain who crosses the sea in search of trade.

She considers a field and buys it, the poem says, and out of her earnings she plants a vineyard, so that the household's wealth grows through her judgment as well as her labour. She sets about her work vigorously, and her arms are strong for her tasks, and she sees that her trading is profitable, and her lamp does not go out at night. A farmer's wife in ancient Israel would have known every one of these tasks, and the poem treats each of them with respect.

In her hand she holds the distaff and grasps the spindle with her fingers, the poem says, and with those same hands she opens her arms to the poor and extends her hands to the needy. When it snows she has no fear for her household, for all of them are clothed in scarlet, which was a warm and costly dye. Her wisdom, the poem suggests, is practical, since she prepares ahead for the cold and also thinks of the people outside her own door who have nothing.

She makes coverings for her bed, the poem says, and she is clothed in fine linen and purple, and her husband is respected at the city gate, where he takes his seat among the elders of the land. She makes linen garments and sells them, and supplies the merchants with sashes, so that her work reaches the market and earns its reward. A household, in this view, is the root of public life, and a man's good name at the gate rests on the order that has been kept at home.

She is clothed with strength and dignity, the poem says, and she can laugh at the days to come, which is one of its most hopeful lines. She speaks with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue, and so the strength of her hands is joined to the kindness of her words. The woman who is not afraid of the future is the one who has prepared for it, and her laughter is the sign of a mind at peace with the work it has done.

She watches over the affairs of her household, the poem says, and does not eat the bread of idleness, and so each of her days is full. Her work is not a burden that crushes her but a pattern of care that makes her home a safe and orderly place. In a book that has said so much against the lazy, it is fitting that its last portrait should be of someone who is never idle, and yet who is never described as anxious.

Her children rise up and call her blessed, the poem says, and her husband also, and he praises her, saying that many women do noble things, but you surpass them all. The praise comes from those who know her best, which is the highest kind of praise, since the people at home are the ones who see everything and cannot be deceived. A good name, which the book prized above riches, is here given to her by her own household.

Charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting, the poem says, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised, and the line draws the whole portrait together. The poem does not say that charm and beauty are wrong, only that they cannot be relied on, and that the lasting thing in a person is the respect for God from which good character grows. With these words the book returns to its motto, the fear of the Lord, which it first stated in the opening verses and has repeated throughout.

Honour her for all that her hands have done, the poem concludes, and let her works bring her praise at the city gate. The gate was where elders sat, trade was done and disputes were settled, and so the praise is to be given in public and in the place where reputations were made. The last line of the poem is thus an act of recognition, which asks the community to say aloud what the household already knows.

A reader who has come this far will have noticed how often the book works in pairs, setting the wise beside the foolish, the honest beside the false, the diligent beside the lazy and the humble beside the proud. Each pair is a fork in the road, and the writers of Proverbs rarely tell the reader which way to turn but only show where each road ends, trusting that anyone who looks will choose well. The device is simple, yet it has kept the book alive for more than two thousand years, because everyone meets those same two roads again and again.

The proverbs describe how life usually goes, and they are not a list of promises that hold in every case, a point that readers of the Hebrew Bible have long understood. The same collection of writings includes the Book of Job, in which a good man suffers, and Ecclesiastes, in which a thoughtful writer wonders whether any effort has lasting value. Together these books suggest that wisdom must include honesty about the limits of rules, and that Proverbs offers the main road while the others walk the hard places beside it.

Over the centuries many readers have read one chapter of Proverbs on each day of the month, since the book has thirty-one chapters, and so they travel from the call of Wisdom to the praise of the capable woman. Such a habit cannot make a person wise, but it does put a few sentences about patience, honesty and kindness in front of him each morning. The book was made for exactly that kind of slow use, since it is made of short sayings that can be read in a moment and thought about all day.

People in many lands and times have collected wise sayings, from the Egyptian teaching mentioned earlier to the folk proverbs of every language, and the experience of ordinary life has taught similar lessons everywhere. Some of the sayings in this book are close to those found in neighbouring nations, which suggests that its writers were part of a wider conversation. Yet the book gives its own foundation for wisdom, which is respect for the Lord, and it is on that point that it differs from a simple collection of good advice.

The book began with Wisdom pictured as a woman who calls out in the streets and the squares, and it ends with a poem about a capable woman who rises early and works with strength and kindness. Many readers see the poem both as a portrait of a real woman and as a picture of Wisdom herself, no longer standing in the market but at home in a household where she is lived out day by day. Whichever reading one prefers, the two women are a pair of bookends, and the book between them is the long answer to the question of how a person can come to know her.

So the book ends as it began, with respect for the Lord as the beginning of wisdom and with the promise that wisdom is something that can be lived. A saying is only words until someone puts it to work, and the proof of the book lies in the ordinary days of people who listen, work, speak truthfully and treat the poor and their neighbours with kindness. Its last picture is not of a scholar or a king but of a woman at her work, and with that picture the Book of Proverbs closes, leaving the reader at the door of the house of wisdom.
